CLAUDE.title: CLAUDE
CLAUDE.content:
CLAUDE.md
This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
Overview
This is an Obsidian personal vault for knowledge management and note-taking. The vault is git-tracked with session-based workflows for collaborative work with Claude Code.
Owner: Tom (tomboo / tom.booster@gmail.com)
Research & Documentation Guidelines
When researching features, syntax, or capabilities of tools and technologies used in this vault, always check official documentation first before performing general web searches.
Official Documentation Sources
Obsidian:

Primary: help.obsidian.md/
Use for: Core features, plugins, syntax, settings, API documentation
Check here first for any Obsidian-related questions

Bases Plugin:

Official help: help.obsidian.md/bases/syntax
Forum: forum.obsidian.md/ (search “Bases”)
Use for: Filter syntax, view configuration, property usage

Research Workflow

Check official docs first - Most accurate, up-to-date information
Search community forums - Real-world examples and solutions
General web search - Only if official sources don’t have the answer
Verify with testing - Test findings in actual vault when possible

Why Official Documentation First?

Accuracy: Official docs reflect current version capabilities
Completeness: Covers all features, not just common use cases
Authority: Direct from developers who built the tool
Efficiency: Faster than sifting through search results

Example: Questions about Bases filter syntax should check help.obsidian.md/bases/syntax before doing web searches, as third-party sources may be outdated or incomplete.
Session Workflow Commands
Six slash commands manage structured work sessions and framework health:
Core Session Commands
/session-start
Begin a new working session. This command:

Syncs with remote (git pull if clean)
Reviews recent commits and last session notes
Verifies git user identity
Checks recent vault modifications
Displays context usage status
Prompts for session focus (Writing, Organization, Projects, Research, Review)

CRITICAL: Stops if uncommitted tracked file changes exist - user must commit or stash first.
/session-commit
Create periodic checkpoint commits during active work:

Analyzes and categorizes changed files
Generates descriptive commit messages
Creates LOCAL commits only (no push)
Use every 15-30 minutes during active sessions
Safety checks for sensitive data

Note: Renamed from /auto-commit in framework v1.0.
/session-end
Conclude a working session with comprehensive tracking:

Displays context usage status
Runs health checks on modified files
Creates detailed session note in _database/database-core/sessions-table/ with format session-YYYYMMDD-NNN.md
Generates ULID for session
Auto-generates commit message from session work
Asks for confirmation before committing
Offers push to remote (no automatic push)

Session notes include: summary, content created, organization work, files modified, next steps.
Context Management Commands
/context-status
Display current context usage and health:

Shows context usage percentage and remaining capacity
Color-coded health indicators (GREEN/YELLOW/RED/CRITICAL)
Breakdown by category (transcript, file reads, tool outputs)
Recommendations based on usage level

Use when: Monitoring during long sessions, before complex operations, when concerned about context.
/session-snapshot
Manually consolidate context with full transparency:

Display before/after context metrics
Preview what will be summarized vs. preserved
User approval required before consolidation
Typical reduction: 50-70% of context usage

Use when: Context reaches 75%+, before major refactoring, after extensive exploration.
Health Monitoring Commands
/health-check
Run comprehensive vault health validation:

Schema compliance (properties, formats, types)
Naming conventions (files, properties, values)
Data integrity (unique UIDs, valid references)
Framework standards adherence
Auto-fix capabilities with user approval

Underlying command: python3 -m _framework.cli.main doctor
Use when: Weekly maintenance, after migrations, before critical work, troubleshooting.
Key Directories
_database/database-core/sessions-table/        # Claude work session tracking notes
_database/database-core/backlog-table/          # Quick-capture ideas, tasks, reminders
_database/database-core/daily-notes-table/     # Auto-generated daily journals (Cmd+D)
_database/database-core/notes-table/           # Casual notes and knowledge
_framework/                     # Framework code (lib, scripts, templates, schemas)
tmp/                            # Archived/temporary content

Obsidian Configuration
Editor Mode: Preview mode (Live Preview disabled)
Links: Wiki-link format [[note]], relative paths
Attachments: Stored in vault root (no dedicated folder)
Daily Notes: Auto-created in _database/database-core/daily-notes-table/ with format YYYY-MM-DD
Theme: Moonstone, 16px base font
Core Plugins Enabled: Daily notes, templates, word count, canvas, properties
Git Workflow
Branch: main (no separate development branches)
What’s Tracked:

All markdown content (notes, projects)
Templates
Session notes in _database/database-core/sessions-table/
.obsidian/ config (except workspace, cache, and most plugin data)
.claude/commands/ slash commands

What’s Ignored:

.obsidian/workspace*.json (local view state)
.obsidian/cache/ (rebuild on open)
Most .obsidian/plugins/*/data.json
OS files (.DS_Store, Thumbs.db)

Commit Philosophy:

Session-based commits through /session-end command
Periodic checkpoint commits via /session-commit during active work
Descriptive messages with file categorization
No automatic pushes - user confirms before pushing to remote

Working with This Vault
Starting Work:

Run /session-start to sync and review recent activity
Confirm focus area when prompted
Begin writing, organizing, or researching

During Work:
4. Use /session-commit every 15-30 minutes for checkpoints
5. Use /context-status to monitor context usage during long sessions
6. Use /session-snapshot if context reaches 75%+ to consolidate
7. Work in Obsidian or edit markdown files directly
Ending Work:
9. Run /session-end to create session notes
10. Review generated commit message and health check results
11. Confirm commit when ready
12. Optionally push to remote
Maintenance:

Run /health-check weekly or after bulk operations
Review and fix any schema or naming issues
Keep vault in healthy state

Template Usage:

Daily notes: Auto-created with Cmd+D using _framework/templates/daily-note-template.md
Projects: Use _framework/templates/project-template.md for new projects
Tasks: Use _framework/templates/task-template.md for task notes

Common Issues
Session tracking:

Session notes go in _database/database-core/sessions-table/
Filename is ULID: 01KF14VPEC8E5W5JER92ECNY0M.md
Always check for existing session notes today before creating new one

Creating new files (v3 pattern):

Generate ULID for filename: 01KF14VPEC8E5W5JER92ECNY0M.md
Store title in frontmatter title: property
Use wikilinks with ULID: [[01KF14VPEC8E5W5JER92ECNY0M]]
Optionally add alias: [[01KF14VPEC8E5W5JER92ECNY0M|Display Title]]

Git conflicts:

/session-start will stop if uncommitted tracked changes exist
User must manually commit or stash before starting new session
This prevents accidental overwrites from git pull

Personal Operating System Framework
This vault implements a Personal Operating System framework (v3.0) for managing knowledge, tasks, and life priorities. The framework uses native Obsidian features enhanced with AI-integrated workflows.
Framework v3 Features
ULID-Based Filenames:

All files use ULID as filename: 01KF14VPEC8E5W5JER92ECNY0M.md
Title stored in frontmatter title: property
Enables stable links even when titles change

SQLite Index:

Derived index at .cache/index.db (gitignored, rebuildable)
Fast queries across 400+ files
Tables: files, tags, links, errors

Lexi CLI:
python3 -m _framework.cli.main <command>
 
# Commands:
lexi doctor      # Vault health summary
lexi index       # Rebuild SQLite index
lexi validate    # Validate against schemas
lexi fix         # Apply auto-fixes (--dry-run to preview)
Split Schemas:

Per-type JSON schemas in _framework/schemas/
Core schema with shared definitions
Type-specific schemas use $ref composition

Framework Documentation
All framework documentation has been migrated to the docs library at _database/database-docs/docs-table/.
Core Standards:

doc-005 - Development Standards (naming conventions, app pattern)
doc-006 - AI Guidelines (session workflows, health monitoring)
doc-009 - Common Properties Schema
doc-010 - App-Specific Schemas

Reference Docs:

doc-007 - Apps Registry
doc-012 - Property Standards
doc-013 - Things 3 Philosophy

App Documentation:

components/sessions/README.md - Sessions app documentation
components/project-management/README.md - Project Management app documentation

Key Concepts
ULID-Based Filenames:

All files use ULID as filename (26-character, Crockford Base32)
Chronologically sortable, globally unique
Auto-generated by AI, no manual user input required
Title stored in frontmatter title: property

Property Schemas:

Common properties: type, title, user, tags, status, created-at
App-specific properties extend common schema
All properties use kebab-case naming

App Pattern:

Every app has: README.md, _index.base (Bases view), property schema
Optional: Slash commands for workflows, templates

Health Monitoring:

AI validates schema compliance at session boundaries
/health-check command for comprehensive vault validation
Auto-fix capabilities with user approval

Context Management:

/context-status for on-demand monitoring
/session-snapshot for manual consolidation
Color-coded warnings (GREEN/YELLOW/RED/CRITICAL)

Framework Philosophy
This is a Personal Operating System designed to:

Maintain focus on life priorities
Prevent distraction and ensure balance
Track progress with data-driven insights
Provide AI-assisted accountability and monitoring

Core Principles:

Simplicity and elegance
Incremental development
AI as core component (proactive, not reactive)
Database-like consistency (ULIDs, schemas)
Single-user optimization (not for sharing)

Current Apps:

Sessions (Active) - Work session tracking with Claude Code
Backlog (Active) - Quick-capture system for ideas, tasks, and reminders

See doc-007 (Apps Registry) in _database/database-docs/docs-table/ for complete app registry and framework documentation.
Using the Backlog App
The Backlog app provides frictionless capture of ideas, tasks, and reminders during any session.
Creating items (natural language):
create backlog item to research Obsidian plugin API tomorrow @learning #technical high 2h
create backlog item to fix critical bug 0 30m @technical #urgent
create backlog item to schedule dentist appointment next week @health-fitness 1h

Natural Language Parsing:
The framework includes an NLP parser that extracts structured data from conversational input:

Dates: tomorrow, next week, next Monday, Jan 15, 2025-01-15
Priorities: critical/0, high/1, medium/2, low/3
Estimates: 30m→PT30M, 2h→P2H, 1.5h→P1H30M (auto-converts to ISO 8601)
Categories: @learning, @health-fitness, @technical (use @ prefix)
Tags: urgent, bug, feature (use # prefix)
Title: Remaining text after extracting metadata

What AI does automatically:

Generates ULID for unique identification
Creates file: _database/database-core/backlog-table/{ULID}.md (ULID as filename)
Parses natural language using NLP parser (_framework/lib/nlp_parser.py)
Extracts and converts metadata (dates, priorities, estimates)
Renders template with structured data (_framework/lib/template_engine.py)
Sets defaults: status=draft, priority=2 if not specified

Item properties:

Required: type, user, title, created-at
Standard: status, priority, category, tags
Optional: estimate, context, related-to, github-issue, deadline

Status values (v3 standard):

draft - Not started, planning stage
active - Currently being worked on
completed - Finished successfully
on-hold - Paused, waiting on something
archived - No longer relevant, kept for reference

Viewing backlog:

Open components/project-management/views/backlog-base.base in Obsidian for filtered views
Views: All Items, Open Items, By Priority, Quick Wins

Common categories:

health-fitness, learning, family-friends, travel-culture
work-projects, personal-development, home-maintenance, creative, technical

Workflow:

During session, ideas pop up → capture immediately with natural language
Weekly review → triage by priority, update status, cancel irrelevant
Work sessions → pull high-priority items, mark in-progress
Completion → mark completed or delete file

GitHub promotion (optional):

Promote backlog items to GitHub Issues when they become projects
Set github-issue property to link them
Use for collaboration, bug tracking, or multi-session features

Task Comment Format
Tasks and backlog items use a standardized comment log at the bottom of the file for tracking updates, completion notes, and cancellation reasons.
Format:
---
## Comments
### YYYY-MM-DD: Title
Comment body text here.
 
### YYYY-MM-DD: Another Update
Additional notes.
Common comment titles:

Completed - Summary of what was done
Canceled - Reason for cancellation
Update - Progress notes or status changes
Blocked - What’s blocking progress
Decision - Important decisions made

Example:
---
## Comments
### 2025-12-25: Completed
All Phase 1 items implemented:
- Created 5 Bases views
- Added 2 dashboard widgets
 
### 2025-12-24: Update
Started implementation, schema complete.
Guidelines:

Place at very end of file, after main content
Use --- horizontal rule to separate from content
Chronological order (newest at bottom)
Keep comments concise but informative

Template System
The framework includes a template engine for automated content generation with variable substitution.
Location: _framework/lib/template_engine.py
Documentation: doc-015 (Template Engine) in docs library
Basic usage:
from lib.template_engine import render_template
 
variables = {
    'user': 'tomboo',
    'title': 'My Task',
    'priority': 1,
    'category': 'technical',
    'estimate': 'P2H',
    'tags': ['framework', 'feature']
}
 
content = render_template('_framework/templates/backlog-template.md', variables)
Supported variables:

{{date}} - Current date (YYYY-MM-DD)
{{timestamp}}, {{created-at}} - ISO 8601 timestamps
{{year}}, {{month}}, {{day}} - Date components
{{user}}, {{title}}, {{type}}, {{tags}}, {{status}} - User-provided values
Any custom variables you pass

Available templates:

_framework/templates/backlog-template.md - Backlog item creation
_framework/templates/session-template.md - Session note creation
_framework/templates/task-template.md - Task creation (existing)

CLI usage:
python3 _framework/lib/template_engine.py _framework/templates/backlog-template.md '{"title": "My Task", "user": "tomboo", "priority": 1}'
See doc-015 (Template Engine) in docs library for complete documentation, examples, and best practices.
Natural Language Parser
The framework includes an NLP parser for extracting structured data from conversational descriptions.
Location: _framework/lib/nlp_parser.py
Documentation: doc-016 (NLP Parser) in docs library
Basic usage:
from lib.nlp_parser import parse_backlog_input
 
text = "research Obsidian API tomorrow @learning #technical high 2h"
result = parse_backlog_input(text)
 
# Returns:
# {
#     'title': 'Research Obsidian API',
#     'date': '2025-12-16',
#     'priority': 1,
#     'category': 'learning',
#     'tags': ['technical'],
#     'estimate': 'P2H'
# }
Supported patterns:

Dates: tomorrow, next week, next Monday, Jan 15, 2025-12-31
Priorities: critical/0, high/1, medium/2, low/3
Estimates: 30m → PT30M, 2h → P2H, 1.5h → P1H30M
Categories: @learning, @health-fitness, @technical
Tags: #bug, #urgent, #feature

CLI usage:
python3 _framework/lib/nlp_parser.py "fix critical bug tomorrow @technical #urgent 30m"
Integration with templates:
from lib.nlp_parser import parse_backlog_input
from lib.template_engine import render_template
 
# Parse natural language
parsed = parse_backlog_input("research API tomorrow @learning high 2h")
 
# Add required fields
parsed['user'] = 'tomboo'
parsed['status'] = 'not-started'
 
# Render template
content = render_template('_framework/templates/backlog-template.md', parsed)
See doc-016 (NLP Parser) in docs library for complete documentation, examples, and edge cases.

_database/content-storage/youtube/2bXHHN.content:
Make 2026 the Year You FINALLY Level Up in Pickleball
Summary
Coach Jess (licensed psychotherapist, pro player, founder of Athena Pickleball) explains why most players don’t improve: they play rec games hoping to get better without intentional practice or implementation plans. This video isn’t about technique—it’s about the framework for actual progress.
Why Players Plateau:

Playing tons of rec games without purpose
Watching YouTube/Instagram without implementation plans
Not seeking proper coaching or feedback

SMART Goal Framework:

Specific - “I want to get better at dinking” not “I want to improve”
Measurable - “Hit 50 forehand dinks in a row under pressure”
Achievable - Know where you’re starting, seek feedback on realistic targets
Realistic - Does this fit your life? (e.g., going pro needs 4-6 hrs/day)
Time-bound - Set 3-6 month horizons, not 3 years

Jess’s Story: Went from 3.5 to winning a 5.0 tournament in ~1 year by: drilling (when nobody did it), seeking coaching (Jesse Irvin taught her the transition zone), working backwards from goal with intermediate tournaments.
Key Tip

You have to be willing to look bad. Tell your partner “I’m working on drops today—they’ll be shaky.” Miss shots rather than avoid practicing them. Stop playing rec just to win if your goal is to improve.

Highlights






























StrategyWhat to DoWhyDrill weeklyEven 10 min before/after rec playMuscle memory needs reps—rec gives 1-2 chances per gamePlay upFind better players, ask for 1-2 gamesSee balls you’re not used to at your levelPlay downPlay with weaker players occasionallyForces strategic thinking, mental toughnessOne focus per sessionPick one thing (footwork, drop, strategy)Too many things = hard to dial in
The Drilling Truth:

“I don’t have time” → Tack 10 min onto rec play, 5x/week = 1 hr/week
“I don’t have partners” → Be brave, ask for numbers, try different people
Rec play alone: shot comes up 1-2x per game. Drilling: hundreds of reps.

Seek Trustworthy Help:

Ignore unsolicited park advice (“everyone has tips for their partners”)
Find coaches/mentors who know the bigger picture
Clinics, lessons, camps > random YouTube without implementation

Action Plan

Write 1-3 goals - Strategic, technical, competitive (who do you want to beat?)
Plan drilling - How will you incorporate it?
Pick one focus - Next rec session, choose ONE thing
Bonus habit - Off-court support (gym, mental game, nutrition)

_database/content-storage/youtube/6qsPHO.title: Build a Foolproof Pickleball Serve from Scratch (Even If You're Just Starting)
_database/content-storage/youtube/6qsPHO.content:
Build a Foolproof Pickleball Serve from Scratch (Even If You’re Just Starting)
Summary
Jess from Athena Pickleball teaches a reliable 3-step serve using a tube as an alignment guide. The serve is the only shot you have complete control over - a good serve sets the tone for the entire point.
The Tube Method (3 Steps):


Position - Place tube pointing where you want to serve. Align hip points along the tube (not toes). Turn slightly to the side to allow weight transfer and power.


Toss/Drop - Release ball right inside the court, just to the right of the tube. This is the point of maximum forward momentum when paddle contacts ball.

Drop serve: Palm down, light touch, drop from shoulder height. Great for beginners - more time.
Toss serve: Low toss (few inches), cradle like an egg, remove arm so ball hangs in contact zone.



Swing - Transfer weight forward → back → forward. Paddle moves along the tube path into the hanging ball.


Why it works: The tube creates a lane your body follows. Works from either side of court - just adjust which foot is back and where tube points.
Key Tip

Height is your friend. You can hit hard and low over the net, but adding height pushes opponents back and makes your serve more effective. Take a little off the power, add arc - easier on you, harder for them.

Highlights

























StepWhat to DoWhySetupAlign hip points along tube, turn slightly sidewaysAllows weight transfer and power generationToss/DropRelease ball just right of tube at contact pointMaximum forward momentum at contactSwingWeight: forward → back → forward along tube pathGenerates power and consistent direction
5 Quick Tips:

Grip - Eastern or slightly further right for topspin
Height - Arc over net pushes opponents deep
Legs first - Power chain: legs → hips → trunk → shoulders
Know your target - Set up body position for intended direction
Keep it simple - When struggling, return to basics: setup, toss, swing path

Beginner Advice: No shame in drop serve - gives you more time to develop timing.

_database/content-storage/youtube/6s6DT1.content:
How to publish your notes for free with Quartz
Summary
Nicole van der Hoeven demonstrates how to use Quartz, a free open-source static site generator, as an alternative to Obsidian Publish. The tutorial covers the complete workflow: cloning Quartz, setting up a GitHub repository, opening it as an Obsidian vault, syncing content, and deploying to GitHub Pages.
The Three Components of Publishing:

Note editor - Obsidian or any markdown editor
Static site generator - Quartz converts markdown to HTML
Hosting provider - GitHub Pages (free)

Key difference from Obsidian Publish: Quartz only handles static site generation, so you need separate tools for editing and hosting. This gives more flexibility but requires more setup.
Key Tip

This isn’t for everyone. Obsidian Publish is still easier for most people at $8/month. Quartz is better if you’re comfortable with terminal, Git/GitHub, and Node.js - or can at least copy-paste commands.

Highlights








































StepActionCommand/NotesInstall QuartzClone and setupgit clone, npm i, npx quartz createGitHub SetupCreate repo, link remotegit remote add origin [url]Obsidian VaultOpen folder in ObsidianConfigure plugins, templatesLocal PreviewBuild and servenpx quartz build --serveDeployGitHub Actions workflowCreate .github/workflows/deploy.yamlCustom DomainOptional DNS setupA records → GitHub IPs
Quick Start Commands
# Clone Quartz
git clone github.com/jackyzha0/quartz.git my-site
cd my-site
 
# Install dependencies
npm i
 
# Initialize
npx quartz create
 
# Link to your GitHub repo
git remote rm origin
git remote add origin github.com/[user]/[repo].git
 
# Sync to GitHub
npx quartz sync --no-pull
 
# Local preview
npx quartz build --serve
Why Quartz?
Pros:

Free and open source
Self-hostable
More customization options
Can be automated in pipelines
Won “Best Tool” in Obsidian Gems of the Year 2023

Cons vs Obsidian Publish:

More complex setup
Requires terminal/Git knowledge
Need to manage hosting separately

Related Resources

Quartz Documentation
Quartz GitHub Repository
Nicole’s blog post

_database/content-storage/youtube/SjZSy8.content:
Building a Second Brain: Capturing, Organizing, and Sharing Knowledge Using Digital Notes
Summary
Tiago Forte presents his “Building a Second Brain” methodology for personal knowledge management. The core problem: we consume 174 newspapers worth of information daily, yet spend 74 hours/year searching for misplaced files. Knowledge management has failed because it’s inherently personal - it loses context when separated from the person who knows it.
The Three Values of a Second Brain:


Remember - Offload detailed memory to digital notes (Evernote, OneNote). These apps are durable (cloud-backed), universal (any file type), centralized (one place), and interconnected (links between notes).


Connect - Find patterns and associations across your notes. Use tags, metadata, image views, and links to reveal relationships. Creativity is fundamentally about recognizing connections between ideas.


Create - Build interpretations backed by supporting evidence. What separates strong interpretation from opinion is proof - examples, statistics, diagrams, quotes. “We only know what we make.”


The goal is to reveal your “personal knowledge landscape” - see what you know and don’t know, freeing mental bandwidth for situational awareness rather than remembering details.
Key Tip

Shift from consuming to creating. The culture of information hyper-consumption (one more article, one more podcast) is counterproductive. If “we only know what we make,” the only way to know more is to make more. Even simple acts like highlighting, drawing diagrams, or presenting at a meetup count as creating knowledge.

_database/content-storage/youtube/h7dbkD.content:
Task Queues Are Replacing Chat Interfaces. Here’s Why (plus a Claude Cowork Demo)
Summary
Nate B Jones analyzes Anthropic’s Claude Cowork launch and its implications for knowledge work. The key insight: Anthropic built and shipped Cowork in just 10 days after noticing developers were using Claude Code for non-coding tasks like organizing expense receipts—revealing Claude Code as a general-purpose agent, not just a coding tool.
Why File System Agents Beat Browser Agents:

Browser agents face adversarial environments (CAPTCHAs, login flows, bot detection)
File system agents operate in cooperative territory—your files don’t fight back
Local machine is non-adversarial, enabling reliable high-stakes work
This is why Cowork processes files first, with web as secondary

The Anti-Slop Architecture:

Work slop = AI output that shifts cognitive burden downstream (receiver must do the thinking sender skipped)
Cowork produces artifacts (working Excel files), not text blobs requiring cleanup
Keeps you in “steering loop” (defining intent) vs “editing loop” (fixing output)
File system sandbox forces specificity—must point at real folders with real files

Task Queues vs Chat:

Chat positions AI as respondent (you ask, it answers)
Task queues position AI as worker (you delegate, it executes, you review)
Enables parallel execution—queue 6 tasks, get 6 threads working simultaneously
Shifts cognitive load from “what do I prompt next?” to “what do I actually need done?”

Implications for 2026:

Desktop native general agent wars coming (Microsoft, Google, OpenAI will respond)
Verification becomes the scarce skill—knowing if output is correct
Junior roles face pressure as execution layer gets automated
AI fluency critical: tools amplify those who know what they’re doing

Key Tip

The chatbot was a transitional form. It existed because LLMs could generate text before they could reliably execute plans. Claude Code proved agentic execution works—Cowork is that capability wrapped in an interface anyone can use. The future is task delegation, not prompt-response cycles.

_database/content-storage/youtube/qazUxt.content:
Give me 10 minutes and I’ll fix your serve forever.
Summary
Kyle Koszuta (A Tour two-time medalist) explains three common pickleball serve mistakes that rob you of power and depth:
Mistake #1: Narrow Base
A narrow stance makes you unstable and prevents weight transfer. Instead, use a “power base” - front foot at 45° toward baseline, back foot parallel. Like a boxer, this lets you shift weight and generate force through the ground.
Mistake #2: Jammed Release (T-Rex Arms)
Keeping the ball too close to your body limits extension and power. Drop the ball further out front (around 45° angle) so you have to reach for it. Like using a driver vs. putter in golf - more distance from body = more clubhead/paddle speed.
Mistake #3: Arm-Only Swing
Swinging harder with just your arm creates “effortful” power. Instead, use full body rotation - like a wind-up toy car releasing energy. Check your finish: if rotating properly, your paddle-side foot will step into the court and your body will face the target.
Key Tip

Don’t overthink topspin. If you fix all three mistakes (wide base + extension + rotation), topspin happens naturally. The paddle face automatically tilts down when you extend out front. Focus on contact point, not paddle angle.

Self-Check: After contact, paddle-side foot should step into court, body faces target.

Transcript: Make 2026 the Year You FINALLY Level Up in Pickleball
2026 is finally going to be the year that you level up in pickle ball, no matter your age, stage, or how long you’ve been playing. This particular video isn’t about technique or strategy, but rather about the steps I want to see you take to actually make improvements in your game and see some real progress. So, in this video, we’re going to talk about goal setting, strategies, and an action plan so that 2026 actually starts out on the right foot. In case you don’t know me yet, I’m Coach Jess, founder of Athena Pickle Ball. I’m a licensed psychotherapist and a pro player and coach. I’ve coached thousands of hours and hundreds of students, helping them level up their game and become the badass players that they are meant to be, both on and off the court. So, let’s talk about why a lot of players don’t improve. The harsh truth is that most people play a ton of wreck games hoping that they’re going to get better. They don’t really play with purpose or they’re watching all the videos on YouTube and those juicy bites on Instagram, but they’re not actually coming up with an implementation plan that’s going to help them get from point A to point B. so that they find themselves doing the same things in the same games and they wonder why 6 months later some of their friends have surpassed them and they’re floundering in the same place. What you need is a framework that includes intentional practice and actionable goals. Okay, I want to start with goal setting and I want to share with you a little bit about my story in my first year of playing pickle ball. When I started, I had a tennis background so that gave me a little bit of a head start. Once I had a couple local 3.5 tournaments under my belt, I made the goal that I wanted to win a 5.0 tournament by the end of 2022. But truthfully, I was sort of floundering around and I knew I was going to have to do something a little bit different if I wanted to meet my goal. So, I came up with a strategy of adding and drilling, which nobody was really doing a few years ago. I found a couple people that were willing to give it a shot. We didn’t really know what we were doing. And I started drilling. And then a really key part of this goal setting journey was that I sought out help and I was lucky enough to find myself in a lesson with Jesse Irvin who taught me something that I had no idea about. Kind of that old you don’t know what you don’t know. She taught me about the transition zone. And this was a key part of me understanding in pickle ball the difference between an intermediate player and an advanced player and beyond. You really had to know that. But nobody I was playing with really was talking about it at the time. There weren’t a ton of YouTube videos like there are now. Maybe that would have been a part of my strategy and my goal setting back then, but there wasn’t much. So, I started working backwards. I set a few tournaments along the way and in early December 2022, I won an A 5.0 tournament. The takeaway here is that if I had just continued just playing Wreck games at the park, I would have probably improved. But I set a plan in place that helped me speed up my progress and it helped me also cut out the things that maybe weren’t as useful. So with that, I want to talk a little bit about your goals. And in case this is a news flash, I’m going to tell you that you are an athlete. I don’t care if you are just starting pickle ball. I don’t care if you’re at a 35 level trying to get to 40 or just beat Mark down at the park. It doesn’t matter. You are an athlete. And if you’re watching this video, you’re coming here because you have some idea in mind of progress that you want to make. And so, we’re going to start with goal setting. But it’s really important that you start to relate to yourself as an athlete who deserves to set these goals. Give yourself permission to move in the direction that you want, no matter what those goals are. So, as of this moment, you are a pickle ball athlete in their goal setting era, and 2026 is your year. I want to introduce you to a goal setting framework that you may have heard of. It’s used by sports psychologists. It’s used by people who work in optimizing human performance and organizational gurus. It’s called smart goal. And we’re going to go through each letter of smart. So, first we have S, which stands for specific. It’s not going to be something like I just want to improve. We’re going to get a little more specific and say something like I want to get better at dinking. Next, we’re to M, which is measurable. So, taking the dink example, what we would be looking at is I want to be able to hit 50 forehand dinks in a row under pressure. Another example might be, I want to enter a 4.0 tournament and I want to win at least half the games. Measurable. You can actually know whether we have done it or we have not done it. Next, we have A, which stands for achievable. Now, this one’s a little bit trickier because pickle ball players, you may have noticed, are notoriously bad at assessing themselves. Often people either think they’re much better or much worse than they are. We want to have an understandable idea of where we’re starting so that we can figure out if we can reasonably get to where we want to go in the specific time frame that we’re going to be talking about. This might mean that you want to seek out some feedback from other people to see if this seems like something that is um challenging but still going to be doable so that you’re not just spinning your wheels and driving yourself nuts. Back to my example, it probably would have been unwise to immediately say I want to win a 5-0 tournament when I didn’t really know how I measured up against other people. Once I had that in place, then it was a little easier to figure out what my path was going to be. So, the R stands for realistic, and this relates to how does this fit into the bigger picture of your life. So, if you’re a full-time parent and you want to go pro, but you don’t have four to six hours a day to be devoting, it may not be the best goal for you to say that I want to be playing pro within a year. So, we want to think about something that’s realistic looking at the big picture of your life. And then finally, we have T. And I think this one’s really important. This is time bound. A spark goal can be a goal of any length of time, but I think it’s important to stay motivated not to pick something that’s like three years in the future. We can dial it back a little bit and pick some things that are maybe 3 months or 6 months. We can see the horizon as we are doing the day-to-day grind of trying to achieve that goal. So to put this all together, an example might be by June 1st, I am going to play and win half the matches in a 4.0 tournament at the local level. A more skills-based goal might be, I want to execute third shot drops at a 70% rate in Wreck games. And you would then over time spend a little bit of time monitoring those games and seeing where are you at and have you gotten to the place of being able to execute seven out of 10 drops? And we would want to set the time limit by let’s just say March 31st. Once you have those goals down, specific, measurable, actionable, realistic, and time bound, [clears throat] now we start to talk about, okay, what are the strategies that I’m going to use in my training to get there? Making the goal is one part of it, but now we actually need a plan. If you want to take this deeper, I created a pickle ball goal setting workbook for 2026. So, if you’re interested in diving a little deeper, you can click the link below and share your email and I’ll send it right over to you. It’s printable, it’s simple, and it’s free. So, check it out. All right, back to strategy. Now that we have some idea of goal setting, I want to talk to you about drilling and making the most of WC play. First, let’s talk about drilling. There’s no secret here that drilling is going to be the fastest way to get you closer to your goals. It might be a painful truth, but it is the truth. And I promise you will improve exponentially if you intentionally drill even one time a week. We can play wreck games all day, but if you’re working on something that we’re trying to improve, you might only see that shot once or twice in a game. Whereas drilling, we’re getting reps and reps and reps and our muscle memory is kicking in. So that when we get to the wreck games, when our body recognizes that shot, we know what to do. In rec play, you just don’t get enough practice in order to have it settle into your system. So, I hear some myths and complaints about this. The first one being that I just don’t have time to drill. I want to dispute that a little bit. You may not have a full hour or an hour and a half to go out and do a separate drill session. But I want to challenge you when you go out to WCK play to find one of the three people that you’re on the court with and ask them if they can spend 10 minutes before or after just drilling one thing. If you can tack on 10 minutes of focused drilling to every wreck game, let’s say you’re playing five, six times a week, that’s an hour of drilling a week that you’ve just kind of snuck in there and that’s a win. I know that there are about a thousand drills out there that you can do and it can get a little bit confusing. But if you just pick one drill to focus on one thing and just dedicate 10 minutes to that after a rec session, that’s a great place to be. If you have more time, wonderful. pick a few drills and just work on the breadand butter shots that you need for your game. That’s going to make a huge difference next year in leveling up. The other thing I hear a lot is that I don’t have anyone to drill with. And I kind of get that. In the beginning, it was hard for me to find people to drill with, too. But there are more people out there as more people are trying to improve that want to drill. So now we have to be a little bit brave in asking for people’s numbers, checking in to see if they want to drill and just dragging some people out there. It might not be a good fit, same as finding a partner to play with, but try a few different people. Drill with people that are willing and then see where it takes you. Not everyone’s going to say yes, but you won’t know until you try. And you might be surprised by how many people actually want to do a drill session. Heck, you might even have a three-person or fourperson drill session lined up once you get the ball rolling. Now that we’ve talked about drilling, let’s talk about actually making wreck play work for you. I have four strategies that I think will be useful to bring with you to open plays, wreck games that you’ve set up, play at the park, etc. Just four strategies will get you thinking in an improver kind of mindset. All right, so strategy number one, and I would argue this is the most important, is that you have to be willing to look bad. This might mean that you tell your partner, “Look, I’m working on drops today. I only usually drive. My drops are a little shaky, but this is what I’m working on.” And then hit trash thirds if you have to. I would rather you miss these balls than not practice them at all, especially if it’s something that you’re actually dedicated to improving. The second strategy is that I want you to play up. So, find better players and try to weasle your way into a few games at a higher level. Don’t expect that people are just going to embrace you with open arms if you’re not quite there, but ask for a game or two. Many people will be willing to say yes, and getting into those better games will help you see more balls that you’re not used to seeing at your level. All right, strategy three. And are you ready for this one? Play down. Playing with people who maybe aren’t quite as strong as you. It forces you to think more strategically and to stay really focused. And that’s great training for your own mental toughness and to really pressure test the shots that you already have. You have to work on staying grounded and hitting more balls even when maybe the other people on the court are not doing quite what you’re used to when you’re playing with people at your level. All right, the final strategy for WCK play is that when you go out on the court, I want you to just pick one thing to focus on. Yes, there’s a lot to work on and I know you want to get there faster, but when you have too many things flying around your brain, it’s hard to remember what you’re working on and then to actually dial it in. So, the third shot drop example, if that’s what you’re working on, we’re thinking about how we’re hitting the drop, how we’re moving our body, positioning. We’re just really dedicating extra mental energy to that one thing in that session and just leave the rest for another time. The takeaway from this is for all of your wreck play, stop playing Wreck just to win. If your goal in 2026 is really to get better, is to really challenge yourself to improve, then you’ve got to be willing to look bad. You’ve got to be willing to lose in a variety of games and a variety of ways. Now that we’ve talked through smart goals and then some actionable steps around drilling and wreck games, I want to just talk about one more thing before we get into your action plan. And that is seek out help. seek out mentors and seek out coaches. And the key here is that they have to be trustworthy. Everybody in the park has all the advice for their partners. And I’m sure you’ve played with them before. It’s the person that’s got unsolicited advice for days. And you don’t want it, and you don’t need it because it may or may not be right. So, I want you to shut out all of the advice that you might be getting from a plethora of people and even from all the YouTube videos and Instagram accounts, and I want you to find out what you need to work on specifically, and then I want you to seek out the help for that specific thing from somebody who can help you. My lesson with Jesse Irvin completely changed the the trajectory of my game. I didn’t know what I didn’t know, and there was nobody really around at an intermediate level to help me out appropriately. And there’s a lot of coaches out there who are at that level that still don’t have a bigger picture. And you just need to make sure you know you can trust the people who are helping you. I think it’s great to get feedback from people you play with about what your weaknesses are because they will tell you what they are targeting when you they are playing you. But then beyond that, when you’re getting the help, go to a clinic, take a lesson, try a camp or workshop. Just keep it simple and go after the bread and butter of what your game is looking for from the right sources. If you can’t work with someone in person or even virtually, then yes, I think the all the instruction that’s all over the internet and I will be adding more YouTube videos to my YouTube channel as well. I think all those things are great, but there’s nothing better than getting an extra pair of eyes on you to really see technically and strategically what you need so that you can craft the right plan to address your weaknesses and help you maximize your particular potential. Okay, now that we’ve gotten through all that, I want to give you a quick action plan for the end of this video. The first is that I want you to consider writing one to three goals. So, this might be a strategic goal, technical goal, and probably a competitive goal. So, what do you want to win? Who do you want to beat? Um, let’s let’s lay that out there. Once you have that, I want you to think about how you’re going to incorporate drilling into your plan. And then the third thing is that the next time you go out for a wreck game, I want you to just choose one focus, whether it’s your footwork, a particular shot, or some idea about how you’re going to execute strategically. The fourth thing I want you to write down is any other habit that you want to incorporate that is a bonus habit. So maybe it’s something offc court, maybe it’s something that you’re working on with your mental game. Just add one more thing that’s going to help you on your journey to whatever that goal is in 2026. 2026 can be the year you finally break through, but you need a plan. You’re allowed to have a plan as a pickle baller. Telling you right now that you are an athlete and you are allowed to treat this as an athlete, even if it doesn’t have anything to do with ever ending up on the pro tour. Take care of your body, go to the gym, eat well, set your goals on court and offc court, and put yourself in the best place that you can be for your journey as a pickle ball athlete. Transcript: Build a Foolproof Pickleball Serve from Scratch (Even If You’re Just Starting)
Hey guys, it’s Jess with Athena Pickle Ball and today I’m going to show you how to get a reliable, powerful serve in under 10 minutes. Most players underestimate the serve, but it’s the only shot in pickle ball that you have complete control over. A good serve sets the tone for the entire point. So, instead of panicking when you step up to the line, I’m going to teach you a serve that is reliable, more consistent, and more powerful, and may even win you some free points. So, before we get into the technical aspects of serving, just a few key principles that you need to know, especially if you’re newer to pickle ball. In pickle ball, the serve is a low to high motion. You have two options for ball release. One is that you can toss the ball out of the air and hit it before the ball hits the ground. The other option is that you can choose to, and it’s called a drop serve, just drop the ball and hit it off the bounce. The other thing that you need to know is that in pickle ball, we serve crosscourt and we’ve got to get the ball past the non volley zone. Deeper is better. So, let’s get into it. I’m going to give you a great serve with only three steps and this tube. Step one is that we’re going to take our handy dandy tube and we’re going to use it to line ourselves up. We want this tube to be pointing where we’re trying to serve the ball. When I set the tube, what this is essentially doing it doing is it is creating this lane along our body where we’re trying to serve the ball. I like to think of my hip points being lined up along the tube. Where my toes are pointing is not so important. I like to just feel relaxed. This is going to allow for that freedom of movement that we’re looking for in order to have that weight transfer from back to front. This tube is essentially providing the guide of where we’re going to hit the ball. If I was serving from a little further out, the angle of the tube is going to be a little bit more that way. And when I come to this side of the court, if I keep the tube like this, I’m serving into the wall. So, what I’m working to do is to line it up this way, moving that right foot back. So now the lane is facing the correct direction. So back to this side of the court. One thing I want to note is that as we’re positioning alongside this tube, we’re really thinking about the hip points creating that lane. I see a lot of people their hips are facing forward essentially kind of locked in horizontally. And what this does is this is going to limit your ability to get power because you’re not able to sink into that back leg. So, it’s a small adjustment, but we’re going to make sure that we’re turned to the side here so that we can maximize the power as we’re serving into the ball. Now that we’re set up properly, we’re going to talk about the toss. The toss, as I mentioned earlier, can be something that’s a toss upward and we’re hitting the ball out of the air. It can be a drop where we’re dropping the ball and hitting it off the bounce. We’re using this tube now as the guide. where I’m looking to drop the ball is going to be right inside the court just to the right of the tube. If I’m tossing the ball, if I was to toss the ball and then drop it, it should end up in the same place. The reason that we’re looking for this visual guide is because this is going to be the point in our swing where we’re going to have maximum momentum moving forward to get that velocity as the paddle is making contact with the ball. So, look, if you’re a beginner, there is no shame in a drop serve. I like the drop serve in the early stages of your pickle ball journey because you just have a lot more time. We want to think about having the ball up, palm down, light touch, and dropping it really from shoulder height so that the ball comes up off the ground enough that we can get under it. Drop serves are great. You can get a lot of power on them. Try it if you’re having trouble with the timing. If you’re doing a toss serve, I want you to think about that toss being very low. Again, cradle it like it’s an egg. We’re not gripping it really tightly. As I’m releasing the ball, I’m simply putting it up in the air just a few inches. And then I’m removing my arm. When I remove my arm, the ball is hanging in that spot. That’s going to be a great contact point for hitting some power. So, now that we’ve positioned our body using the tube and we know where we’re releasing the ball, the last thing we need to do is to move that paddle along this tube. This is the swing path we’ve created. And we’re going to do that by transferring our weight. So, I like to tell my students to think about starting with their weight forward. And as they’re tossing or dropping the ball, they’re sinking into that back leg. And then the last piece of the puzzle is to transfer our weight from back to front right into the ball that’s waiting for us. Okay? Forward, back, forward. And you didn’t see that ball, but I moved my paddle right along this tube and the ball went exactly where the tube is pointing. So, most people tend to feel that one side’s a little easier than the other. But with this tube method, you can essentially just set yourself up. And it’s going to be easy from either side. When I set the tube here, it’s the difference between my right foot being back or being this direction. So, I have it kind of behind or I’m facing that way. When I step up to the tube, if my toss is in the right place and I have this swing path, the ball’s always going to go in the direction that we want it to. Now that we’ve covered the basics, here are five quick tips to maximize your serve. Tip one, I prefer an eastern grip or even a little further over to the right. This is going to give you great top spin and allow you to direct the serve properly using that tube setup. Tip two, height is your friend. I can hit the ball as hard as I want this low over the net, but remember that we’re trying to keep our opponents deep off the return. If I take a little bit off, but give the ball a little more height over the net, it’s a lot easier on me, and it’s going to push our opponents back and make our serve that much more effective. Tip three is that power comes from your legs first. So when we start forward and we sink back into that back leg, I want you really pushing off and feeling your momentum drive forward off that leg into the hips, then the trunk, then the shoulders. So tip four is know where you’re planning to serve the ball. I’m not just serving willy-nilly. I’m thinking about where my swing path and my follow through is going to be so I can get the ball in the direction that I want it to go. If I’m going more middle, I’m going to set up my body a little bit to the right here so that I can finish my paddle towards where I’m trying to hit it. If I was trying to serve it wide, I’d position a little bit more that direction and I’m going to finish my paddle now towards that corner of the court. So, set your intention, visualize, and think about where you’re trying to hit the ball and go for it. Tip five is to just keep it simple. If you’re finding that the balls are not going where you want them to go, you’re losing power, come back to that setup, the toss or the drop, and that swing path. And from there, you can iterate. Simple, simple, simple. This will give you the best chances of hitting a consistent, powerful serve every time. Thank you guys for watching. My goal in these videos is to give you useful tools you can take straight to the court. Drop your questions in the comments. I love answering them and hearing from you guys. And make sure to like this video and subscribe for more coaching and all things Athena pickle

_database/content-storage/youtube/transc.title: Transcript: How to publish your notes for free with Quartz
_database/content-storage/youtube/transc.content:
Most of the notes that I write are published online and I’ve mentioned in previous videos that the service that I used to do that is Obsidian’s own paid service Obsidian Publish. But Publish has its own faults - it’s paid for starters and there’s no way to self-host it. It’s also been very slow for me for quite some time. I also wish that there were more options for customizing it and I wish that I could include it in some sort of automated pipeline.
In this video I’m going to talk about a free alternative to Obsidian Publish and how to set that up from scratch. It’s called Quartz.
What is Quartz?
Quartz is not actually a community plugin - it is a separate tool that happens to work really well with Obsidian and that’s because it was designed with Obsidian in mind. But you don’t have to use Obsidian to use it.
Now when you’re looking at publishing markdown notes there are actually three components that you’re looking at:


The tool that creates/edits notes - stores those notes as markdown. You can use Obsidian for this but you could use a text editor or an IDE like VS Code as well.


The static site generator - turns markdown into HTML. HTML is a better format, it’s more portable for viewing online and has become the standard for most websites.


The hosting provider - putting it online means putting it on someone’s server. That could be yours but it could be somebody else’s.


Now with Obsidian Publish it does all three of these roles, but Quartz only does the middle part - the static site generation. Which means you’ll still need to use something to generate your markdown notes and you’ll still need to have a hosting provider.
The Workflow
Here’s the workflow that I’m going to show you:

Obsidian to generate the source text (markdown files)
Quartz as my static site generator
GitHub Pages as my hosting provider

And just to give you a sneak peek, this is the end result - a site that I’ve created using my notes generated by Obsidian and also hosted on GitHub Pages. Just like you might expect with Obsidian Publish, clicking on the links works just as well. There’s even a graph view.
Who This Is For
I got to say up front that this really isn’t for everyone. I think for most people Obsidian Publish is still the easier option - it is convenient, it’s right within Obsidian, and $8 a month really isn’t a lot to pay for a tool if you use it a lot like I do.
However if you do want to do it this way I think you’re going to find it easier if you:

Are familiar or comfortable with working in a terminal
Have worked with Git and GitHub before
Are comfortable with Node.js or npm or NVM (or at least can copy and paste commands)

Step 1: Download and Install Quartz
Quartz is open source so we just need to clone the repository that it’s in and then save that locally so that we can work with it. We’re also going to need to install some dependencies for it.
git clone github.com/jackyzha0/quartz.git
mv quartz doing-it-in-public
cd doing-it-in-public
npm i
npx quartz create
When asked how to initialize the content, choose “empty quartz” for a brand new setup. Choose “treat links as shortest path” for most Obsidian vaults.
Step 2: Set Up the GitHub Repository
Sign up for a GitHub account if you don’t already have one. Create a new repository - do not initialize it with a README, license, or .gitignore.
git remote rm origin
git remote add origin [your-repo-url]
npx quartz sync --no-pull
Step 3: Make it an Obsidian Vault
Open the folder/repository in Obsidian. You can configure Obsidian to look the way that you want. Install plugins like Longform if needed.
For authoring content, Quartz recommends a standard format with frontmatter:

title
draft
tags

Step 4: Sync Local to GitHub
npx quartz sync
This pushes changes to GitHub.
Step 5: Build and Preview Locally
npx quartz build --serve
This starts a local server so you can preview your site.
Step 6: Host Online with GitHub Pages
Create a new file .github/workflows/deploy.yaml with the GitHub Actions workflow from the Quartz documentation.
Then in your repository settings:

Go to Settings → Pages
Under Source, select “GitHub Actions”
Run npx quartz sync

Your site will be available at [username].github.io/[repo-name]
Step 7 (Optional): Custom Domain
If you want to use a custom domain:

In your domain DNS settings, add A records pointing to GitHub’s IP addresses
In GitHub repository settings → Pages, add your custom domain
Enable “Enforce HTTPS”

DNS propagation can take time - sometimes up to an hour or more.
Closing Thoughts
Quartz just won the annual Obsidian Gems of the Year awards for 2023 under “Best Tool.”
Does that mean I’m giving up Obsidian Publish? No. I believe in using the best tool for the job and there are a lot of jobs. I still plan to use Obsidian Publish for the majority of my notes. For work I use other static site generators like Hugo and Gatsby.
Consider supporting the developer Jackie Zhao on GitHub if you like Quartz.

10 days. That’s how long it took Anthropic to build and ship Claude Co-work after they noticed something their product team was not expecting. _database/database-core/notes-table/01KE.title: How to Give Your AI Agent Long-Term Memory
_database/database-core/notes-table/01KE.content:
ttps://youtu.be/cWBVMEHPgQU
How to Give Your AI Agent Long-Term Memory
Here’s a clear, structured summary of “How to Give Your AI Agent Long-Term Memory”, with key topics and timestamps, based directly on the video transcript.

High-level Summary
The video explains why built-in AI agent to-do lists are fundamentally broken (ephemeral, unshareable, and fragile across context resets) and introduces Beads as a persistent, Git-backed memory system for AI coding agents.
Beads replaces ad-hoc markdown task lists with a structured issue graph stored in SQLite + JSONL, enabling agents to reason over tasks, priorities, blockers, and dependencies across long time horizons—and even across multiple developers and machines.

Key Topics & Timestamps
🧠 The Core Problem: Ephemeral Agent To-Dos
0:00 – 1:20


AI agent task lists only exist inside a single session.


They can’t be shared, versioned, or trusted long-term.


Markdown workarounds drift, bloat context, and break agent alignment.



💡 Introducing Beads: Persistent Agent Memory
1:20 – 2:00


Beads is a “memory upgrade” for coding agents.


Tasks live outside the LLM context window.


Designed for long-horizon, multi-session work.



🗂️ How Beads Works Under the Hood
2:00 – 3:40


Local SQLite database for fast access.


JSONL file committed to Git for sharing and history.


Git hooks keep memory in sync across pulls/pushes.


Supports assignments, priorities, blockers, epics, and dependencies.



⚙️ Installation & Initialization
3:40 – 6:00


Install via npm, curl, or brew.


bd init sets up the Beads directory and database.


bd doctor fixes missing hooks or config issues.


Project-specific prefixes keep issues namespaced.



🤖 Onboarding AI Agents (Claude, Copilot, etc.)
6:00 – 8:20


bd onboard updates agent instruction files.


Agents are explicitly told:


Don’t use internal to-do lists.


Don’t create markdown task files.


Use Beads for all task tracking.




Works across multiple AI coding tools.



🧩 Tasks, Dependencies, and Focused Context
8:20 – 10:30


Tasks can block or depend on other tasks.


Agents only load the current relevant issue into context.


Avoids bloated prompts and irrelevant history.



📋 CLI Task Management
10:30 – 12:30


bd create → create tasks (via CLI or AI).


bd list → show all tasks.


bd ready → show tasks with no blockers.


Enables agents to autonomously choose valid next work.



🧪 Turning Tool Output into Tasks
12:30 – 14:30


Run linters/tests (e.g., TypeScript, pnpm).


Automatically convert errors into Beads tasks.


Keeps diagnostics out of markdown and inside structured memory.



🖥️ UI Options: Web, TUI, and Kanban
14:30 – 18:00


Optional Web UI (beads-ui).


Terminal UI (bv) with:


Task lists


Priority indicators


Dependency graphs


Kanban views




Excellent visibility for large projects.



🤯 Autonomous Bug Fixing with Live State Updates
18:00 – 21:00


Ask the AI to:


Find all open bugs


Fix them one by one




Tasks automatically move through:

Ready → In Progress → Done



Status updates happen in real time.



🔌 Sentry Integration via MCP (Major Highlight)
21:00 – 26:00


Pull production errors from Sentry.


Auto-create Beads tasks with:


Error URLs


Stack traces


Root-cause analysis (via Sentry Seer AI)




Agents can fix bugs without rediscovering context.



✈️ “Landing the Plane”: Clean Task Completion
26:00 – 28:30


Documentation includes end-of-task checklists:


Run tests


Run linting


Push to Git




Prevents half-finished agent work.



🎯 Final Takeaways
28:30 – End


Beads solves:


Task drift


Context loss


Markdown sprawl




Enables reliable, scalable AI agent workflows.


Especially valuable for:


Long-running projects


Teams


Autonomous agents





One-Sentence Verdict
Beads turns AI agents from short-term interns into long-term collaborators by giving them durable, structured memory that survives context resets, Git pulls, and real-world complexity.
If you’d like, I can also:


Compare Beads to markdown-based agent workflows


Explain how this fits into RAG vs task memory


Map this to your own long-term “second brain” or agent systems

_database/database-core/notes-table/01KF.title: Natural Language Parser Architecture
_database/database-core/notes-table/01KF.content:
Natural Language Parser Architecture
Documentation of the _framework/lib/nlp_parser.py module for extracting structured data from conversational input.
Overview
The NLP parser is a regex-based Python module that extracts structured data from free-form natural language text. It’s designed for backlog/task item creation but could be extended to other use cases.
Main Function
from lib.nlp_parser import parse_backlog_input
 
result = parse_backlog_input("research Obsidian API tomorrow @learning #technical high 2h")
Output:
{
    'title': 'Research Obsidian API',
    'date': '2025-12-29',        # tomorrow parsed
    'priority': 'p1',             # "high" → p1
    'category': 'learning',       # @learning
    'tags': ['technical'],        # #technical
    'estimate': 'P2H'             # 2h → ISO 8601
}
Parser Pipeline
The parser chains 5 extraction functions sequentially, each consuming its matched text and passing the remainder to the next:









































FunctionPatternExample InputOutputparse_date_expression()Relative/absolute datestomorrow, next Monday, Jan 152025-12-29parse_priority()Priority keywordshigh, critical, p0p1, p0parse_estimate()Time durations2h, 30m, 1dP2H, PT30M, P1Dparse_category()@-prefixed@learninglearningparse_tags()-prefixed#technical #writing['technical', 'writing']
Chaining Pattern
remaining_text = text
date, remaining_text = parse_date_expression(remaining_text)
priority, remaining_text = parse_priority(remaining_text)
estimate, remaining_text = parse_estimate(remaining_text)
category, remaining_text = parse_category(remaining_text)
tags, remaining_text = parse_tags(remaining_text)
title = clean_title(remaining_text)  # Whatever's left becomes the title
Each function returns a tuple of (extracted_value, remaining_text). The remaining text (after all extractions) becomes the title.
Date Parsing Details
Supports multiple date formats:
Relative dates:

tomorrow, today
next week, next month
in 3 days, in 2 weeks
next Monday, next Friday

Absolute dates:

Jan 15, January 15th
2025-01-15 (ISO format)
12/15, 12/15/2025 (US format)

Priority Mapping

























KeywordsPriority Codecritical, urgent, p0p0high, important, p1p1medium, normal, p2p2low, p3p3
Estimate Conversion
Converts human-readable durations to ISO 8601:





























InputOutput15m, 30mPT15M, PT30M1h, 2hP1H, P2H1.5hP1H30M1d, 2dP1D, P2D1wP7D
CLI Usage
python3 _framework/lib/nlp_parser.py "fix bug tomorrow high 30m @dev #backend"
Current Limitations

Designed specifically for backlog/task items
Not connected to any “framework commands” - it’s a data extraction utility
Regex-based (not ML/AI) - handles common patterns but not complex sentences

File Location
_framework/lib/nlp_parser.py
Related

README - Framework overview
README - Todo app that could use parsed data

Framework v2 Architecture
This document describes the v2 architecture for the Personal Operating System framework.
Overview
Framework v2 introduces:

Multiple databases with semantic names
JSON Schema for validation
Components (renamed from apps) with explicit dependencies
Self-contained databases for portability

Key Concepts
Databases
Each database is a self-contained unit with:

schema.json - Defines all tables and properties
*-table/ directories - Contains markdown files

Components
Components are the UI layer that:

Declare which databases they use via manifest.json
Contain views, dashboards, and documentation
May include automation scripts (future)

Schema Validation
JSON Schema provides:

Machine-readable property definitions
Automated validation at scale
Template generation from schema

Directory Structure
vault/
├── _database/
│   ├── database-core/
│   │   ├── schema.json
│   │   └── *-table/
│   └── database-docs/
│       ├── schema.json
│       └── docs-table/
└── components/
    ├── project-management/
    │   └── manifest.json
    └── docs/
        └── manifest.json

Related

Docs Component README
README
