_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDE.title: Framework Changes: Dec 24-25, 2025
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDE.content:
Framework Changes: Dec 24-25, 2025
Purpose: Checklist of framework changes from vault-personal-tom to evaluate for porting to lexi-you-da-hoe.
Sessions Analyzed: 13 sessions (20251224-001 through 20251225-005)

1. Schema Changes (Things 3 Alignment)
Status Value Simplification

 Tasks: not-started/in-progress → open, cancelled → canceled
 Projects: active/planning → open, cancelled → canceled
 Backlog: Same pattern as Tasks
 Areas: Remove status property entirely (areas are perpetually active)

Completion Tracking

 Add completed-at property (auto-set when status → completed)
 Add canceled-at property (auto-set when status → canceled)
 Add to: Tasks, Projects, Backlog

Property Renaming (Tasks)

 scheduled-date → when (intention: “I plan to work on this”)
 due-date → deadline (obligation: “This must be done by”)

Property Removal

 Remove date from Tasks (redundant with created-at)
 Remove context from Tasks (low value)
 Remove actual-duration from Tasks (rarely used)
 Remove modified-at from ALL files (use file.mtime instead)
 Remove status from Areas (perpetually active)

Property Additions

 Add repeat to Tasks (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, after-completion)
 Add checklist to Tasks (subtask items)
 Add project-type to Projects (finite | ongoing)

Property Order Standard
uid, user, type, title, status, priority, description, when, deadline,
repeat, estimate, project, area, checklist, tags, created-at


2. File Naming Convention
Sequential Naming Migration

 Tasks: task-YYYYMMDD-###.md → task-###.md
 Backlog: backlog-YYYYMMDD-###.md → backlog-###.md
 Subscriptions: subscription-YYYYMMDD-###.md → subscription-###.md
 Sessions: Keep session-YYYYMMDD-###.md (date is semantically important)

Benefits:

Shorter filenames (9 chars saved per file)
Easier references: “task 7” vs “task-20251217-007”
Cleaner wikilinks: [[01KCPDVSFB19AJ4EHZYJAT9H78]] vs [[task-20251217-005]]

Migration Script: scripts/migrate-to-sequential-naming.py

3. App Structure Changes
App Consolidation

 Merge apps/tasks/ into apps/project-management/
 Merge apps/backlog/ into apps/project-management/
 Create unified umbrella app with sub-views

App Flattening (Simple Apps)

 Remove views/ subdirectory (files go directly in app folder)
 Remove dashboards/ subdirectory
 Keep nested structure only for complex apps (project-management)

Notes App

 Create Notes app for casual note capture
 Status workflow: draft → active → archived
 Replace inbox/ folder with status: draft workflow

Backend Structure

 Move daily-notes/ → _database/database-core/daily-notes-table/
 Create _database/database-core/notes-table/
 Ensure all data tables are in _database/database-core/*-table/ format


4. Bases View Improvements
Syntax Fixes (Critical)

 Use filters: not filter: (plural is correct)
 Use today() function, not date(now)
 Remove formulas: sections (not yet supported)
 Remove summaries: sections (not yet supported)
 Add file.name as first column in all views (enables clickable rows)

Things 3 Views (Tasks)

 Inbox: Uncategorized tasks (no project)
 Today: when == today() OR deadline == today() OR status == 'in-progress'
 Upcoming: Next 7 days, grouped by when
 Someday: Organized but unscheduled
 Anytime (By Project): Grouped by project
 Anytime (By Area): Grouped by area
 Logbook: Completed tasks, sorted by completed-at DESC
 All Tasks: Unfiltered master view

Dashboard Views

 Sessions dashboard (last 5 sessions)
 Tasks dashboard (high-priority, sorted by priority)
 Backlog dashboard (p0/p1 items only)


5. Documentation & Standards
New Standards Documents

 standards/property-standards.md - Comprehensive property schema reference
 standards/migration-guide.md - Migration workflow with rollback procedures
 standards/things3-philosophy.md - Things 3 design philosophy (512 lines)
 standards/projects-areas-schema-analysis.md - Detailed schema comparison

CLAUDE.md Additions

 Research & Documentation Guidelines (check official docs first)
 Task Comment Format (## Comments / ### YYYY-MM-DD: Title)
 Link Standards (wiki-links for internal, markdown for external)

Template Updates

 Add ## Comments section to task-template.md
 Add ## Comments section to backlog-template.md
 Update templates with current schema (remove deprecated properties)


6. Tooling & Scripts
Migration Scripts

 scripts/add-uids.py - Add UIDs to files missing them
 scripts/standardize-properties.py - Property ordering and format
 scripts/validate-schema.py - Schema validation with detailed reports
 scripts/migrate-to-sequential-naming.py - File naming migration
 scripts/migrate-tasks-to-things3.py - Task schema migration
 scripts/migrate-areas.py - Area schema updates
 scripts/migrate-projects.py - Project schema updates
 scripts/migrate-backlog.py - Backlog status alignment

Health Check Enhancements

 Update validator to accept new status values (open, canceled)
 Validate completion timestamps on completed/canceled items
 Check for deprecated properties

Testing Infrastructure

 tests/test_backend_tables.py - Comprehensive tests for all backend tables
 Schema validation tests for all app types
 Integration tests for backlog and sessions


7. Slash Command Improvements
/session-start

 Dynamic focus suggestions based on recent activity
 Analyze last session’s Next Steps
 Check recent backlog/tasks for pending work
 Generate contextual recommendations vs static options

/session-end

 6-step Next Steps generation strategy
 Context-aware task recommendations
 Auto-generate commit message from session work

/health-check

 Integration with migration scripts
 Auto-fix capabilities with user approval
 Validation of new schema properties


8. Home Dashboard
Embedded Bases Views

 Quick Actions section
 Database Apps with metrics
 Recent Activity (sessions, tasks, backlog)
 Vault Metrics (file counts, app stats)

Link Standards

 Use wiki-links for internal files (not markdown links)
 Use plain text for directory paths
 Use markdown links only for external URLs


Priority Recommendations for lexi-you-da-hoe
High Priority (Core Schema)

Status value simplification (Things 3 alignment)
Completion tracking (completed-at, canceled-at)
when/deadline property renaming
Remove modified-at (use file.mtime)

Medium Priority (Structure)

Sequential file naming
Bases view syntax fixes
App consolidation/flattening
Home dashboard improvements

Lower Priority (Nice to Have)

Notes app
Migration scripts
Testing infrastructure
Documentation standards


Files Changed Summary











































































SessionFiles ChangedKey Changes0013/session-start enhancement00216Property standards, dashboard, migration scripts003104Sequential naming migration (98 files renamed)0045Migration documentation00556Tasks Things 3 schema migration00671Views, project organization, normalization007155Complete Things 3 alignment (131 files migrated)0088Phase 2 documentation (1,351 lines)20251225-00156Bases syntax fixes, project split20251225-00227Notes app, vault structure, tests20251225-003225+Remove modified-at from entire vault20251225-00415Task triage, link standards20251225-00544Status spelling, completion timestamps
Total: ~780+ file changes over 13 sessions

Key Architectural Decisions

Things 3 Philosophy: Simple status model (open/completed/canceled), when vs deadline semantics
Status-Based Workflow: Use status properties instead of folder-based organization (e.g., status: draft vs inbox/ folder)
Flat App Structure: Simple apps don’t need views/ and dashboards/ subdirectories
Sequential Naming: Stable IDs for long-lived content, date-based only for sessions
Official Docs First: Always check official documentation before web searches
Wiki-Links Standard: Use wiki-links for all internal references


Vault Comparison: vault-personal-tom vs lexi-you-da-hoe
Structural Overview



































Aspectvault-personal-tomlexi-you-da-hoePurposePersonal OS (tasks, projects, notes)Creative writing (manuscript, beats, characters)Apps4 (Sessions, PM, Subscriptions, Notes)7 (Sessions, Tasks, Beats, Characters, Locations, Library, Manuscript)Backend Tables9 tables6 tablesTask Count92 tasks19 tasksSession Count38 sessions19 sessions
Schema Differences















































Propertyvault-personal-tomlexi-you-da-hoeNotesTask Statusopen, completed, canceled (string)true, false (boolean)Major differencePriorityp0, p1, p2, p3high, medium, lowDifferent conventionsSchedulingwhen + deadlinedue-date onlyLexi simplermodified-atRemoved (use file.mtime)Still presentvault-personal-tom newercompleted-atPresent on completed itemsPresent but inconsistentcanceled-atPresent on canceled itemsNot used
Structure Differences



































Aspectvault-personal-tomlexi-you-da-hoeFile namingSequential (task-###.md)Sequential (task-NNN.md)inbox/ folderRemoved (use status: draft)Still existsApp structureFlattened (most apps)Nested (all apps)App consolidationtasks+backlog → PMSeparate appsBases syntaxFixed (filters:, today())Unknown state
What Lexi Already Has

 Sequential file naming for tasks, beats
 ULID-based unique identifiers
 Property order standards (uid first, timestamps last)
 Session workflow commands (/session-start, /session-end, etc.)
 Home dashboard with embedded Bases
 Health check system
 property-standards.md documentation

What Lexi Is Missing

 String status values (uses boolean)
 when property (scheduling intention)
 deadline property rename (still uses due-date)
 completed-at on all completed items
 canceled-at property
 Things 3 view patterns (Inbox, Today, Upcoming, Someday)
 Removal of modified-at
 Removal of inbox/ folder
 Task comment format (## Comments)


Detailed Recommendations for lexi-you-da-hoe
MUST APPLY (High Impact, Low Risk)
1. Remove modified-at Property
Effort: Low (script-based)
Impact: High (schema simplification)
Rationale: file.mtime is automatic and maintenance-free. Lexi has 200+ files with modified-at that requires manual updates.
# Migration approach
# 1. Create script to remove modified-at from all files
# 2. Update templates to remove modified-at
# 3. Update property-standards.md
2. Bases Syntax Audit & Fix
Effort: Low
Impact: Critical (views may not work correctly)
Rationale: vault-personal-tom discovered filters: (not filter:), today() (not date(now)), and that formulas: aren’t supported.
Check in lexi:

 All .base files use filters: (plural)
 Date filtering uses today() function
 No unsupported formulas: sections
 All views have file.name as first column

3. Task Comment Format
Effort: Low
Impact: Medium (consistency)
Rationale: Standardized format for tracking task completion notes.
---
## Comments
### YYYY-MM-DD: Completed
Summary of what was done.
SHOULD APPLY (Medium Impact)
4. Task Status: Boolean → String
Effort: Medium (migration script needed)
Impact: High (enables Things 3 views)
Rationale: Boolean status (true/false) doesn’t support intermediate states or canceled items.
Current lexi:
status: true    # completed
status: false   # not completed
Proposed:
status: open        # active task
status: completed   # done
status: canceled    # abandoned
Migration:

status: true → status: completed
status: false → status: open

5. Add when Property
Effort: Medium
Impact: High (Things 3 semantics)
Rationale: Separates “when I intend to work” from “when it’s due”.
Current lexi: Only due-date
Proposed: when (intention) + deadline (obligation)
Migration:

Rename due-date → deadline
Add when as optional property
Most lexi tasks don’t have due-date anyway (9/19 are null)

6. Completion Tracking
Effort: Low
Impact: Medium (better history)
Rationale: Know when tasks were completed for analytics.
Add to tasks:

completed-at - Auto-set when status → completed
canceled-at - Auto-set when status → canceled

CONSIDER APPLYING (Lower Priority)
7. Remove inbox/ Folder
Effort: Medium
Impact: Low (structural cleanup)
Rationale: Status-based workflow (status: draft) is cleaner than folder-based.
Current lexi: 17 files in inbox/
Migration: Move to appropriate locations, use status properties
8. App Flattening
Effort: Low
Impact: Low (simplification)
Rationale: Simple apps don’t need views/ subdirectories.
Affected apps in lexi:

apps/beats/ (already flat)
apps/characters/
apps/locations/
apps/library/
apps/manuscript/
apps/sessions/
apps/tasks/

9. Priority Alignment
Effort: Low
Impact: Low (convention change)
Current: high, medium, low
Proposed: p0, p1, p2, p3
Recommendation: Keep lexi’s current format. It’s clear and works for a writing vault with fewer tasks.
DO NOT APPLY
App Consolidation (tasks+backlog → PM)
Reason: Lexi doesn’t have a backlog app. Task structure is simpler and appropriate for writing context.
Notes App
Reason: Lexi has drafts/ for WIP content and a different organizational model focused on writing artifacts (beats, characters, locations).
Things 3 Views (Full Set)
Reason: Lexi’s task model is simpler. 19 tasks don’t need 8 views. Keep existing 5-view structure (Active, By Priority, By Status, Completed, All Tasks).

Migration Priority Order for lexi-you-da-hoe
Phase 1: Quick Wins (1-2 hours)

Audit and fix Bases syntax (filters:, today(), file.name)
Remove modified-at from templates
Add Task Comment format to CLAUDE.md

Phase 2: Schema Migration (2-4 hours)

Task status: boolean → string (open/completed/canceled)
Rename due-date → deadline
Add when property (optional)
Add completed-at to completed tasks
Remove modified-at from all files

Phase 3: Cleanup (Optional, 1-2 hours)

Remove inbox/ folder (migrate files)
App structure review (flatten if desired)

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDE.title: Framework v2: Multi-Vault Platform Architecture PRD
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDE.content:
Framework v2: Multi-Vault Platform Architecture
Status: Planning
Created: 2025-12-26
Last Updated: 2025-12-26

Executive Summary
Redesign the Personal Operating System framework as a portable, scalable platform that can be deployed to multiple project vaults with different requirements, supporting both technical power users and non-technical end users at scale.

Context
The Lexi Ecosystem (3-tier)
lexi-depot (stable backend - Firebase/Firestore)
  ↓ provides data storage
lexi-vault (CLI orchestration - rapid iteration)
  ↓ manages vaults
Project Vaults (Obsidian vaults - where framework lives)
  - vault-personal-tom (Tom's personal OS)
  - lexi-you-da-hoe (Lexi's writing vault)
  - Future: additional project vaults

Framework v2 is vault-internal infrastructure that provides database-like structure, schema validation, and component patterns within Obsidian project vaults.
Scale Requirements
Current (vault-personal-tom):

220 files across 8 backend tables
Single user (Tom - technical)
Active development/iteration

Near-term (migration targets):

Notion migration: Thousands of pages with integrations and automation
Lexi’s writing vault: ~8,000 scenes written over 20-30 years
Multiple novels and projects
Non-technical user (Lexi)

Total scale: 10,000+ items across multiple vaults
User Profiles



































AspectTom (Developer)Lexi (End User)InterfaceCLI, slash commands, Python, APIsNLP, AI conversations, natural languageUpdatesContinuous, bleeding edgeInfrequent, stable releases onlyToleranceBreaking changes OKMinimal churn requiredComplexityExposed, full powerHidden, “it just works”RoleDevelopment environmentProduction deployment

Problem Statement
Current v1 Limitations

Not designed for multi-vault deployment - Tightly coupled to single vault
No formal schema system - Ad-hoc Python validation, prone to drift
No clear separation - Apps mix UI and data concerns
Not scalable - 8,000 files will strain current structure
Not portable - Can’t easily share framework between vaults
No release model - Can’t have stable (Lexi) + dev (Tom) versions

Design Review Findings
Initial critique (assuming 220 files, single user):

Over-engineered
ULIDs overkill
Too much validation
Fighting Obsidian’s simplicity

Revised assessment (with 10K+ files, two vaults, release model):

✅ ULIDs justified (bulk imports, cross-vault uniqueness)
✅ Schema validation essential (can’t manually review 8K files)
✅ Multiple databases necessary (different vault types)
✅ Database-like approach appropriate at this scale
✅ Python tooling needed for bulk operations


Framework v2 Architecture
Core Concepts
1. Components (renamed from “apps”)

UI/presentation layer
Declare database/table dependencies in manifest
Can use one or more databases
Future: Python automation scripts

2. Databases (semantic names)

Self-contained with schema.json
Multiple databases per vault (e.g., core, docs, writing)
Each database has multiple tables
Portable across vaults

3. JSON Schema

Machine-readable schema per database
Defines all tables in that database
Validates frontmatter properties
Enables template generation
Self-contained for portability

4. Shared Framework

Base property templates (uid, created-at, timestamps)
Validation tooling (Python libs)
NLP parser, template engine
Slash commands
Health checks

Architecture Diagram
Framework Layer (shared via release)
├── Base schema templates
├── Validation library (lib/)
├── Template engine
├── NLP parser
├── Slash commands (.claude/commands/)
└── Health check tools

Vault Layer (instance-specific)
├── vault-personal-tom/
│   ├── databases/
│   │   ├── core/
│   │   │   ├── schema.json (defines tasks, projects, sessions, etc.)
│   │   │   ├── tasks-table/
│   │   │   ├── projects-table/
│   │   │   └── sessions-table/
│   │   └── docs/
│   │       ├── schema.json (defines docs, contacts, etc.)
│   │       ├── docs-table/
│   │       └── contacts-table/
│   └── components/
│       ├── project-management/
│       │   ├── manifest.json (declares: uses core db, tables: tasks/projects/areas)
│       │   └── views/
│       └── docs/
│           ├── manifest.json (declares: uses docs db)
│           └── views/
│
└── lexi-you-da-hoe/
    ├── databases/
    │   ├── writing/
    │   │   ├── schema.json (defines scenes, characters, novels, etc.)
    │   │   ├── scenes-table/ (8,000+ files)
    │   │   ├── characters-table/
    │   │   └── novels-table/
    │   └── library/
    │       ├── schema.json (synced from depot)
    │       └── scenes-table/
    └── components/
        └── manuscript-manager/
            ├── manifest.json
            └── views/

Key Design Decisions
Schema Inheritance & Portability

Each database schema is self-contained (no external references)
Template schema exists as source of truth for base properties
New databases are generated from template (gets base properties)
Portability: Copy database folder = copy everything it needs

Release Model

Tom’s vault = development environment
Periodic stable releases exported to Lexi’s vault
Version pinning - Lexi’s vault declares framework version
Migration scripts provided with releases
Changelog documents breaking changes

Component Manifest Format
{
  "name": "docs",
  "version": "1.0",
  "databases": ["docs"],
  "tables": ["docs-table", "contacts-table"],
  "description": "Documentation and contacts management"
}

v2 vs v1 Comparison


















































Aspectv1 (Current)v2 (Proposed)Data layer_database/database-core/*-table/databases/{name}/ with schemaUI layerapps/components/SchemaMarkdown docs + Python validatorsJSON Schema per databaseValidationAd-hoc PythonSchema-drivenMulti-vaultNot supportedCore design principlePortabilityCopy files manuallyCopy database folderDependenciesImplicitExplicit in manifestRelease modelNoneDev → Stable releases

Implementation Approach
Phase 1: Proof of Concept

Create database-docs/ with schema.json
Test on real data (copy existing items for validation)
Create components/docs/ with manifest
Validate pattern works before full migration

Phase 2: Migration Strategy

database-core/ = existing _database/database-core/ tables + schema
Update existing components to use manifests
Gradual migration, maintain compatibility

Phase 3: Lexi Vault

Design database-writing/ schema for scenes/characters/novels
Test with subset of 8,000 scenes
Stable release process


Open Questions


Database naming: Semantic (core, docs, writing) or numbered (database-001)?

Decision: Semantic names for clarity



Schema granularity: One schema per database, or per table?

Decision: One per database using type property to differentiate tables



Template sharing: How are base properties shared across databases?

Decision: Template schema + generation, self-contained result



First test case: New database or migrate existing?

Decision: Test on copy of real data to validate upward compatibility



Framework distribution: Git submodule, copy/sync, monorepo, or package?

Decision: Copy with version pinning (Tom iterates, Lexi gets releases)




Success Metrics
Technical

✅ Single database folder is fully portable
✅ Schema validates 8,000+ files without errors
✅ Template generation creates valid items
✅ Migration preserves all existing data

User Experience

✅ Tom can iterate rapidly on dev vault
✅ Lexi receives stable, tested releases
✅ Natural language commands work (NLP layer)
✅ Complexity hidden from end user


Next Steps

Read official JSON Schema docs - Research best practices
Design database-docs schema.json - First test case
Create component manifest spec - Define structure
Test on real data - Copy existing items, validate
Document migration path - v1 → v2 upgrade process


Related Documents

/Users/tom/Projects/lexi/lexi-vault/docs/architecture.md - Lexi ecosystem overview
/Users/tom/Projects/lexi/lexi-vault/CLAUDE.md - lexi-vault project context
standards/apps.md - Current v1 app registry
standards/development.md - Current v1 development patterns
Design review findings (this session, 2025-12-26)


Backlog Items Created

backlog-051.md - Research formal schema validation with JSON Schema (p1, 2h)
backlog-052.md - Create a contacts database (p2)
backlog-053.md - Distinguish between subscriptions and monthly payments/utilities (p2)

Framework v2 Architecture Plan
Overview
Evolve the Personal Operating System framework from v1 (single vault, implicit structure) to v2 (multi-vault platform with explicit schemas and portable databases).

User Profiles






























AspectTom (Developer)Lexi (End User)InterfaceCLI, slash commands, Python, APIsNLP, AI conversationsUpdatesContinuous, bleeding edgeInfrequent, stable releasesToleranceBreaking changes OKMinimal churn requiredComplexityExposedHidden
Design Principles

Databases are self-contained and portable
Components declare explicit dependencies
JSON Schema drives validation and template generation
Framework is reusable across vaults with different content


Architecture
Directory Structure
vault/
├── _framework/                    # Shared framework (versioned)
│   ├── version.json               # Framework version
│   ├── schemas/

│   │   ├── tasks-table/

│   │   └── ...

├── components/                    # UI layer (renamed from apps/)

│   │   ├── views/

│       ├── manifest.json
│       └── views/
│
├── .claude/commands/              # Slash commands

Database Structure
Each database is self-contained:

├── sessions-table/

├── tasks-table/

├── projects-table/
│   └── project-website.md
├── areas-table/
│   └── area-work.md
└── backlog-table/
    └── backlog-001.md

JSON Schema Format
{
  "$schema": "json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "database-core-schema",
  "title": "Core Database Schema",
  "description": "Schema for tasks, projects, areas, backlog, sessions",
 
  "definitions": {
    "uid": {
      "type": "string",
      "pattern": "^[0-9A-Z]{26}$",
      "description": "26-character ULID"
    },
    "timestamp": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "date-time"
    },
    "base-properties": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "uid": { "$ref": "#/definitions/uid" },
        "type": { "type": "string" },
        "user": { "type": "string" },
        "created-at": { "$ref": "#/definitions/timestamp" }
      },
      "required": ["uid", "type"]
    }
  },
 
  "allOf": [
    { "$ref": "#/definitions/base-properties" },
    {
      "if": { "properties": { "type": { "const": "task" } } },
      "then": {
        "properties": {
          "title": { "type": "string" },
          "status": { "enum": ["open", "completed", "canceled"] },
          "priority": { "enum": ["0", "1", "2", "3"] },
          "when": { "type": "string", "format": "date" },
          "deadline": { "type": "string", "format": "date" }
        },
        "required": ["title", "status"]
      }
    },
    {
      "if": { "properties": { "type": { "const": "doc" } } },
      "then": {
        "properties": {
          "title": { "type": "string" },
          "status": { "enum": ["draft", "active", "archived"] },
          "slug": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["title", "status"]
      }
    }
  ]
}
Component Manifest
{
  "name": "project-management",
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "description": "Task, project, and area management",
  "databases": ["database-core"],
  "tables": [
    "tasks-table",
    "projects-table",
    "areas-table",
    "backlog-table"
  ],
  "views": [
    "views/tasks.base",
    "views/projects.base",
    "views/inbox.base",
    "views/today.base"
  ],
  "dashboards": [
    "dashboards/home.base"
  ]
}

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.title: Development Standards
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Development Standards
Standards for developing and maintaining the Personal Operating System framework.
Philosophy
Core Principles

Consistency over convenience - Same patterns everywhere
Simplicity over flexibility - Fewer options, less confusion
Obsidian-native - Work with Obsidian, not against it
AI-friendly - Easy for Claude to parse and generate
Human-readable - Clear to humans in raw markdown

Single-User Optimization
This framework is designed for personal use by a single user. This allows:

No multi-user permissions or sharing concerns
Simpler file naming without collision worries
Direct file editing without merge conflicts
Personalized workflows and automation

Naming Conventions
File Naming
Pattern: {type}-{identifier}.md or {type}-YYYYMMDD-NNN.md
Rules:

Use kebab-case (lowercase with hyphens)
No spaces, underscores, or special characters
Descriptive but concise

Examples:
backlog-20251213-001.md     # Date-based identifier
session-20251213-001.md     # Date-based identifier
project-website-redesign.md # Slug-based identifier (long-lived entities)
area-work.md                # Slug-based identifier

Exceptions (allowed uppercase):

README.md - Standard documentation file
CLAUDE.md - Claude Code instructions
PRD.md - Product Requirements Document

Directory Naming
Rules:

Use kebab-case for all directories
Pluralize table directories (e.g., sessions-table/, backlog-table/)
Use descriptive names

Examples:
planning/sessions/           # Session notes
planning/backlog/            # Backlog items
templates/                   # Reusable templates
standards/                   # Framework standards

Property Naming
Rules:

Use kebab-case for all YAML frontmatter properties
Be descriptive but concise
Use consistent terminology across apps

Examples:
# Good
created-at: 2025-12-13T15:30:00-08:00
session-number: 1
due-date: 2025-12-20
 
# Bad
createdAt: ...       # camelCase not allowed
session_number: ...  # snake_case not allowed
dueDate: ...         # camelCase not allowed
Property Value Naming
Rules:

Use kebab-case for enum/status values
Use lowercase for consistency
Exception: Priority uses pN format (p0, p1, p2, p3)

Examples:
# Good
status: not-started
status: in-progress
priority: 1
category: health-fitness
 
# Bad
status: NotStarted    # PascalCase not allowed
status: in_progress   # snake_case not allowed
priority: high        # Use p0-p3 instead
Tag Naming
Rules:

Use kebab-case for all tags
Be specific but not too long
Use consistent vocabulary

Examples:
# Good
tags: [framework, session, planning]
tags: [health-fitness, exercise]
 
# Bad
tags: [Framework, Session]  # No capitalization
tags: [health_fitness]      # No underscores
Directory Structure
Current Structure
vault-personal-tom/
├── .obsidian/              # Obsidian configuration (partially tracked)
├── planning/               # Session notes, backlog
│   ├── sessions/          # Work session tracking
│   └── backlog/           # Quick-capture items
├── templates/              # Reusable note templates
├── standards/              # Framework documentation
├── tmp/                    # Temporary/archived content
├── CLAUDE.md               # Claude Code instructions
└── [content directories]   # Your actual vault content

App Pattern (Database-App Separation)
Overview:
Apps in the framework separate concerns into two layers:

Database Layer - Where data lives (planning/{app}/)
App Layer - Views and UI (apps/{app}/)

Structure:
planning/                    # Database layer
├── sessions/               # Session data
│   └── session-YYYYMMDD-NNN.md
└── backlog/                # Backlog data
    └── backlog-YYYYMMDD-NNN.md

apps/                        # App layer
├── sessions/               # Sessions app
│   ├── README.md           # Documentation
│   ├── _index.base         # Bases view
│   └── dashboard.md        # Optional dashboard
└── backlog/                # Backlog app
    ├── README.md           # Documentation
    └── _index.base         # Bases view

Benefits:

Clear separation of data and presentation
Multiple apps can share data
Easier to migrate or reorganize
Consistent pattern across all apps

ULID Identifiers
What is ULID?
ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) is a 26-character identifier that is:

Unique - Globally unique, no collisions
Sortable - Chronologically sortable by string comparison
URL-safe - Base32 encoded, no special characters

Format
01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV
└─────────┘└─────────────┘
 Timestamp    Randomness
 (10 chars)   (16 chars)

Usage in Framework
Every entity has a uid property:
 
Properties:

Auto-generated by AI when creating items
Never manually entered by user
Used for cross-referencing between files
Enables reliable linking even after renames

Generation
AI generates ULIDs using Python:
from ulid import ULID
uid = str(ULID())
# Returns: "01KAGWC2WNMNDGH2PP6NYZY8BY"
Note: The ulid-py package must be installed:
pip install python-ulid
Common Property Patterns
Timestamps
Created-at Pattern:
created-at: 2025-12-13T15:30:00-08:00

ISO 8601 format
Includes timezone offset
Set once when item created
Never modified

Date Pattern:
 

YYYY-MM-DD format
Primary date of item
May be creation date or relevant date

Status Values
Standard statuses across apps:
# Backlog/Tasks
status: not-started
status: in-progress
status: completed
status: cancelled
 
# Sessions (implicit - sessions don't have status)
# Areas
status: active
status: paused
status: archived
Priority Values
Standard priority scale:
priority: 0  # Critical - must do immediately
priority: 1  # High - important, do soon
priority: 2  # Medium - normal priority (default)
priority: 3  # Low - nice to have
User Property
Identifies item owner:
user: tomboo

Single-user system, always same value
Required for all items
Enables future multi-user if needed

Wikilinks and References
Link Format
Standard wikilink:
[[path/to/file|Display Text]]
Examples:
[[01KCC813T7P5NKXVRJXF284WQT|Session 1]]
[[01KCCGZM8NQRS4TV6WXY9ZAB2C|Bug Fix]]
Relationship Properties
Single reference:
project: "[[planning/projects/project-001|Website Redesign]]"
Multiple references:
related-sessions:
  - "[[01KCC813T7P5NKXVRJXF284WQT]]"
  - "[[01KCC8MFQ6VQTCD430C3KRFWX4]]"
Best Practices

Always use display text for clarity
Use relative paths from vault root
Quote wikilinks in YAML to prevent parsing issues
Keep paths short but descriptive

Template Usage
Template Location
All templates stored in templates/ directory:
templates/
├── backlog-template.md     # Backlog item template
├── session-template.md     # Session note template
├── daily-note-template.md  # Daily note template
└── project-template.md     # Project template

Template Variables
Templates use {{variable}} syntax:
---
user: {{user}}
---
 
# {{title}}
Template Best Practices

Include all required properties in frontmatter
Use consistent section structure in body
Document template in README of relevant app
Update templates when schema changes

Git Practices
What to Commit
Always commit:

All markdown content
Templates
Standards documentation
Session notes

Never commit:

.obsidian/workspace*.json (local state)
.obsidian/cache/ (rebuild on open)
Sensitive data (credentials, API keys)

Commit Messages
Format:
Type: Brief description

Optional longer explanation.

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Types:

Session: Session work (Session 2025-12-13-1: Framework Planning)
Add: New feature or content
Update: Modification to existing
Fix: Bug fix or correction
Refactor: Code/structure improvement
Docs: Documentation only

Branch Strategy
Simple approach:

Single main branch
No feature branches (single user)
Commit frequently during sessions
Push at session end

Bases Views
Column Order
Rule: file.name must always be the first column in all Bases table views.
Rationale:

Provides consistent navigation across all database views
file.name is the primary identifier and link to open the note
Users expect the clickable link in a predictable position

Example:
views:
  - type: table
    name: All Items
    order:
      - file.name      # Always first
      - title
      - status
      - priority
      - date
Applies to:

All .base files in components/
All _index.base files in database tables
Both views and dashboards

Health Monitoring
What AI Validates
At session boundaries:

Schema compliance (required properties, types)
Naming conventions (kebab-case)
ULID format and uniqueness
Date formats
Link integrity

Health Check Command
/health-check

Runs comprehensive validation with optional auto-fix.
Auto-Fix Capability
With user permission, AI can:

Add missing required properties
Fix format violations
Generate missing UIDs
Rename files to conventions

Best Practices Summary
Do

Use kebab-case everywhere
Include all required properties
Let AI generate UIDs
Use templates for consistency
Commit frequently during sessions
Run health checks regularly

Don’t

Use camelCase or snake_case
Manually create UIDs
Skip required properties
Modify templates without updating docs
Commit without reviewing changes
Ignore health check warnings

Related Documentation

standards/schemas/common-properties.md - Property definitions
standards/schemas/app-schemas.md - App-specific schemas
standards/ai-guidelines.md - AI responsibilities
standards/testing.md - Testing standards


Comments
2025-12-26: Migrated
Migrated from standards/development.md to docs library.

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.title: AI Guidelines
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
AI Guidelines
Guidelines for AI (Claude) behavior in the Personal Operating System framework.
Philosophy
AI as Core Component
AI is not an afterthought—it’s a core component of the Personal Operating System. Claude:

Proactively maintains vault health
Enforces consistency and standards
Reduces friction in workflows
Provides accountability and tracking

Proactive, Not Reactive
AI should anticipate needs rather than wait for explicit requests:

Validate schemas at session boundaries
Suggest health checks when issues detected
Offer to fix problems automatically
Remind about uncommitted work

Respect User Autonomy
While being proactive, AI must:

Never make changes without permission
Always explain what it will do
Provide opt-out for suggestions
Respect user preferences

Session Boundaries
Session Start
Trigger: /session-start command
AI Responsibilities:

Check git status for uncommitted changes
Sync with remote if clean
Review recent commits
Read most recent session note
Display context usage
Ask for session focus

Output Format:
Context: 39K/200K (19% used, 161K remaining) ✓

Recent commits:
- [commit hash] commit message
- [commit hash] commit message

Last session: Session 2025-12-13-1
- Focus: Organization, Planning
- Summary: [brief summary]

What would you like to focus on?

Session End
Trigger: /session-end command
AI Responsibilities:

Create comprehensive session note
Run health checks on modified files
Display context usage
Generate commit message
Ask for commit confirmation
Offer push to remote

Session Note Structure:

Summary of work completed
Content created
Organization work
Files modified
Next steps

During Session
Periodic Responsibilities:

Monitor context usage
Track modifications
Maintain awareness of session focus
Offer checkpoint commits

Health Monitoring
Proactive Validation
AI validates at natural boundaries:

Session start/end
After bulk operations
When creating new items
Before commits

What to Validate
Schema Compliance:

Required properties present
Property types correct
Enum values valid
Date formats correct

Naming Conventions:

Files use kebab-case
Properties use kebab-case
Values use kebab-case (with exceptions)

Data Integrity:

UIDs are unique
References resolve
No orphan files

Health Check Command
Trigger: /health-check
Output Format:
✓ Backlog: 15 items validated
✓ Sessions: 8 notes validated
⚠ Tasks: 2 issues found
  - task-001.md: Missing uid property
  - task-003.md: Invalid priority value "high"

Would you like me to fix these automatically?

Auto-Fix Capability
With user confirmation, AI can:

Add missing required properties
Fix invalid enum values
Generate missing UIDs
Rename files to conventions
Update timestamp formats

Never auto-fix without asking.
Context Management
Tracking Context Usage
AI should:

Display context at session boundaries
Warn when approaching limits
Suggest consolidation when needed
Track usage trends

Context Display Format
Context: 39K/200K (19% used, 161K remaining) ✓

Warning Levels:

GREEN (0-50%): ✓ Healthy
YELLOW (51-75%): ⚠ Monitor
RED (76-90%): 🔴 Consider snapshot
CRITICAL (91-100%): 🚨 Consolidation recommended

Context Conservation
Best Practices:

Summarize large file contents
Avoid re-reading unchanged files
Use targeted searches over full scans
Consolidate when approaching limits

Entity Creation
Generating UIDs
When creating any entity (backlog item, session note, etc.):
from ulid import ULID
uid = str(ULID())
Rules:

Always generate fresh ULID
Never reuse UIDs
Include in frontmatter immediately
Verify uniqueness if concerned

Applying Templates
When creating new items:

Load appropriate template
Substitute variables
Generate ULID
Set timestamps
Apply user defaults

Natural Language Parsing
For commands like “create backlog item to fix bug tomorrow high priority”:

Extract intent (create backlog item)
Parse title (“fix bug”)
Extract date (“tomorrow” → YYYY-MM-DD)
Extract priority (“high” → p1)
Apply defaults for missing fields
Create item with full schema

Commit Guidelines
Checkpoint Commits
Trigger: /session-commit or /auto-commit
Format:
Auto-commit: [Category] - [Brief description]

Files: [list of changed files]

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Session End Commits
Format:
Session YYYY-MM-DD-N: [Session Title]

Summary:
- [Key accomplishment 1]
- [Key accomplishment 2]

Files:
- [Category]: [file count] files

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Never Commit

Sensitive data (credentials, keys)
Temporary files (unless intentional)
Workspace state files
Cache files

Error Handling
Graceful Degradation
When operations fail:

Explain what happened
Suggest alternatives
Offer to try again
Preserve work in progress

Validation Errors
When validation fails:

List all issues found
Prioritize by severity
Offer to fix automatically
Explain what each fix does

Git Conflicts
When conflicts occur:

Stop and explain
Show conflicting changes
Ask user to resolve
Never force-push without explicit permission

Slash Commands
Command Behavior
All slash commands should:

Acknowledge the command
Show what will happen
Execute the operation
Report results
Ask for next steps if applicable

Error Recovery
If a slash command fails:

Explain the failure

Offer to retry

Follow templates consistently
Ask before making changes
Display context status regularly
Offer auto-fix with explanation

Don’t

Modify files without permission
Skip required properties

Force-push without asking
Ignore validation errors
Let context overflow

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.title: Testing Standards
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Testing Standards
Standards for testing the Personal Operating System framework.
Overview
The testing framework validates schema compliance, naming conventions, and data integrity across the vault. Tests are written in Python using pytest.
Philosophy
What to Test

Schema validation - Required properties, types, formats
Naming conventions - kebab-case enforcement, file patterns
ULID format - Valid Base32, 26 characters, uniqueness
Deterministic validation - Rules that have clear right/wrong answers
Data integrity - No duplicate UIDs, valid references

What NOT to Test

Obsidian functionality - Trust the Obsidian app
Git operations - Trust git
Markdown rendering - Not our concern
AI natural language parsing - Too variable, non-deterministic
User content - Don’t validate creative writing, notes, etc.

Testing Pyramid
         /\
        /  \  Integration (vault-wide validation)
       /____\
      /      \
     /  Unit  \ (schema validators, ULID utils)
    /__________\
   /   Fixtures \
  / (Valid/Invalid)\
 /__________________\

Focus: Bottom two layers (fixtures and unit tests)
Framework: Python + pytest
Why Python + pytest?

Readable tests - Clear assertion syntax
YAML parsing - Native support for frontmatter
Parameterization - Easy to test all vault files
Great error messages - Shows exactly what failed
No compilation - Fast feedback loop

Installation
Option 1: Global install (simple)
pip install pytest pyyaml
Option 2: Virtual environment (isolated)
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate  # On macOS/Linux
pip install pytest pyyaml
Verify installation:
pytest --version
# Should show: pytest 7.x.x or higher
Directory Structure
vault-personal-tom/
├── tests/
│   ├── conftest.py                    # Pytest fixtures (imports from lib/)
│   ├── test_schema_validation.py     # Schema compliance tests
│   ├── test_ulid.py                   # ULID format and uniqueness
│   ├── test_naming_conventions.py    # File/dir/property naming
│   ├── test_integration_backlog.py   # Integration tests for backlog items
│   ├── test_integration_sessions.py  # Integration tests for session notes
│   └── fixtures/
│       ├── valid/                     # Known-good examples
│       │   ├── backlog-valid.md
│       │   └── session-valid.md
│       └── invalid/                   # Known-bad examples
│           ├── backlog-no-uid.md
│           └── backlog-wrong-priority.md
├── lib/                               # Shared validation library
│   ├── __init__.py                    # Package exports
│   ├── validators.py                  # Core validators (ULID, kebab-case, dates)
│   └── schema_validators.py          # App-specific validators
├── pytest.ini                         # pytest configuration
└── standards/
    └── testing.md                     # This file

Running Tests
Basic Usage
Run all tests:
pytest tests/
Run specific test file:
pytest tests/test_schema_validation.py
Run specific test function:
pytest tests/test_schema_validation.py::test_backlog_has_required_properties
Verbose output:
pytest -v
Stop on first failure:
pytest -x
Show print statements:
pytest -s
Advanced Usage
Run only fast tests (skip integration):
pytest -m "not integration"
Run with coverage:
pip install pytest-cov
pytest --cov=lib --cov=tests --cov-report=term
Watch mode (auto-rerun on changes):
pip install pytest-watch
ptw tests/
Writing Tests
Test File Naming

Pattern: test_<component>.py
Examples: test_schema_validation.py, test_ulid.py
Location: tests/ directory
Convention: One test file per logical component

Test Function Naming

Pattern: test_<what_is_being_tested>()
Examples:

test_backlog_has_required_properties()
test_ulid_format_valid()
test_priority_values_are_valid()


Be descriptive: Test name should explain what passes/fails

Basic Test Structure
import pytest
from conftest import parse_markdown_frontmatter, is_valid_ulid
 
def test_backlog_has_required_properties():
    """Backlog items must have uid, date, user, title."""
    # Arrange
    backlog = parse_markdown_frontmatter("tests/fixtures/valid/backlog-valid.md")
 
    # Assert
    assert "uid" in backlog
    assert "date" in backlog
    assert "user" in backlog
    assert "title" in backlog
Using Fixtures
Load fixture in test:
def test_with_fixture(valid_backlog):
    """Use pytest fixture defined in conftest.py"""
    assert valid_backlog["priority"] in ["0", "1", "2", "3"]
Define fixture in conftest.py:
@pytest.fixture
def valid_backlog():
    """Load valid backlog fixture."""
    return parse_markdown_frontmatter("tests/fixtures/valid/backlog-valid.md")
Parameterized Tests
Test all vault files:
import glob
import pytest
 
@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "backlog_file",
    glob.glob("_database/database-core/backlog-table/backlog-*.md")
)
def test_all_backlog_items_valid(backlog_file):
    """Validate every backlog item in vault."""
    item = parse_markdown_frontmatter(backlog_file)
 
    assert "uid" in item
    assert "priority" in item
    assert item["priority"] in ["0", "1", "2", "3"]
Shared Validation Library (lib/)
The lib/ directory contains reusable validation functions used by both tests and /health-check.
lib/validators.py - Core Validators
Contains low-level validation functions:
from lib.validators import (
    parse_markdown_frontmatter,  # Parse YAML frontmatter from markdown files
    is_valid_ulid,               # Validate ULID format (26 chars, Base32)
    is_kebab_case,               # Check kebab-case naming
    is_valid_date,               # Validate YYYY-MM-DD or datetime.date
    is_valid_iso_timestamp       # Validate ISO 8601 timestamps
)
lib/schema_validators.py - App-Specific Validators
Contains high-level schema validation functions for specific apps:
from lib.schema_validators import (
    validate_backlog_item,        # Returns (is_valid, errors)
    validate_session_note,        # Returns (is_valid, errors)
    validate_all_backlog_items,   # Returns {file: (is_valid, errors)}
    validate_all_session_notes    # Returns {file: (is_valid, errors)}
)
Best Practices
Keep Tests Fast

Use fixtures, not real vault files (for unit tests)
Parameterized tests for integration
Mock expensive operations
Run integration tests separately (pytest -m integration)

Keep Tests Isolated

Each test should be independent
Don’t rely on test execution order
Clean up temp files in teardown
Use fixtures for shared setup

Make Tests Readable

Descriptive test names
Clear assertion messages
One logical assertion per test
Comment complex test logic

Maintain Fixtures

Update fixtures when schema changes
Keep valid fixtures truly valid
Document why invalid fixtures are invalid
Use realistic data in fixtures

Common Properties - Common property definitions
App Schemas - App-specific schemas
AI Guidelines - AI health check responsibilities

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.title: Common Properties Schema
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Common Properties Schema
Shared properties used across all apps in the Personal Operating System framework.
Overview
All app items (sessions, backlog items, etc.) extend this common schema. This ensures consistency, enables cross-app queries, and provides standard metadata for all content.
Standard Property Order
All properties MUST appear in this canonical order in frontmatter:

title - Human-readable title (first for readability)
type - Document type
user - Creator username
Type-specific properties (status, priority, relationships, etc.)
tags - Tag array
created-at - Creation timestamp (second to last)
updated-at - Last modified timestamp (always last)

Key principle: Title first for human readability, timestamps last for consistency.
Required Properties
uid

Type: String (ULID)
Format: 26-character Base32 encoded ULID
Example: 01KAGWC2WNMNDGH2PP6NYZY8BY
Purpose: Unique identifier for the item
Generation: Auto-generated by AI, never manual

date

Type: Date
Format: YYYY-MM-DD
Example: 2025-12-13
Purpose: Primary date associated with the item

user

Type: String
Format: Git username (kebab-case preferred)
Example: tomboo
Purpose: Owner/creator of the item

type

Type: String (enumerated)
Format: kebab-case
Example: task, project, session, backlog
Purpose: Identifies which table/entity the note belongs to

Standard Properties
tags

Type: List of Strings
Format: Each tag in kebab-case
Example: [framework, planning, session]
Purpose: Categorization and filtering

status

Type: String (enumerated)
Format: kebab-case
Values: not-started, in-progress, completed, blocked, cancelled, someday
Default: not-started

created-at

Type: DateTime
Format: ISO 8601 with timezone
Example: 2025-12-13T14:30:00-08:00
Generation: Set once at file creation, never modified

updated-at

Type: DateTime
Format: ISO 8601 with timezone
Example: 2025-12-13T16:45:00-08:00
Purpose: Tracks when file content was last modified
Generation: Auto-populated by “Update Frontmatter Modified Date” plugin
Behavior: Updates on Obsidian file events (captures both user edits and external changes)
Exclusions: _framework/, tmp/ folders excluded from auto-update
Note: External edits (e.g., Claude Code) trigger update when file is opened in Obsidian

Optional Common Properties
priority

Type: String (enumerated)
Format: p0, p1, p2, p3
Values:

p0 - Critical
p1 - High
p2 - Medium (default)
p3 - Low



category

Type: String or List of Strings
Format: kebab-case
Example: health-fitness or [learning, technical]

related-to

Type: List of Wiki-links
Format: ["[[file-name]]", "[[another-file]]"]

Relationship Properties
Pattern: Wikilinks-Only
Use Obsidian’s native wikilinks for all relationships:
related-projects:
  - "[[../projects-table/project-001|Website Redesign]]"
Naming Conventions

Prefix: related- for most relationships
Plural: Use plural form for array relationships
Kebab-case: related-projects, parent-task

Best Practices

Use Obsidian’s autocomplete to create wikilinks
Include display text after | for clarity
Use relative paths for portability
Always use arrays, even for single relationships

Validation Rules
Required Fields
All app items MUST have:

uid (valid ULID)
date (valid ISO 8601 date)
user (non-empty string)
type (valid table/entity name)

Format Validation

UIDs: Exactly 26 characters, Base32 alphabet
Dates: YYYY-MM-DD format
DateTimes: ISO 8601 with timezone
Kebab-case: Lowercase, hyphens only

Development Standards - Naming conventions
App Schemas - App-specific property definitions
Apps Registry - Registry of all apps

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Migration Guide
Guide for migrating existing vault files to match property standards.
Current Status
✅ Migration Complete
All app tables already have UIDs and follow property standards.
Migration Scripts
Three scripts are available for future schema changes:
1. add-uids.py
Purpose: Add ULID to files missing uid property
python3 scripts/add-uids.py --app tasks --dry-run
python3 scripts/add-uids.py --app all --validate
2. standardize-properties.py
Purpose: Reorder properties to standard order
python3 scripts/standardize-properties.py --app tasks --dry-run
python3 scripts/standardize-properties.py --app all
3. validate-schema.py
Purpose: Validate property schemas
python3 scripts/validate-schema.py --app all --verbose
Pre-Migration Checklist

Backup vault with git tag
Test with dry-run first
Review sample files manually

Migration Process
Recommended: One app at a time
python3 scripts/add-uids.py --app projects --validate
git diff _database/database-core/projects-table/
git commit -m "Add UIDs to projects app"
Post-Migration Validation
python3 scripts/validate-schema.py --app all --verbose
python3 health-check.py
Sequential Naming Migration (Dec 2024)
Migrated 101 files from date-based to sequential naming:

44 tasks: task-YYYYMMDD-###.md → task-###.md
50 backlog: backlog-YYYYMMDD-###.md → backlog-###.md
4 subscriptions: date-based → sequential

Script: scripts/migrate-to-sequential-naming.py
Why Sequential:

Shorter filenames
Easier verbal references
Stable IDs for long-lived content

Why Keep Sessions Date-Based:

Date is semantically important
Multiple sessions per day need indexing

Best Practices

Always use dry-run first
One app at a time for easier review
Commit between apps
Validate after migration
Test in Obsidian

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.title: Things 3 Philosophy Guide
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Things 3 Philosophy Guide
Design philosophy behind Things 3 and how the Personal OS framework applies these principles.
Why Things 3?
Things 3 is a task management app with 15+ years of battle-tested design decisions. Personal OS adopts its core philosophy while extending it with Obsidian’s knowledge management, AI workflows, and markdown storage.
Core Philosophy
1. Simplicity Over Features
Things 3: Fewer features, executed perfectly
Personal OS: Minimal property schemas, sensible defaults, natural language input
2. Areas → Projects → Tasks Hierarchy

Areas: Ongoing life responsibilities (no end date)
Projects: Finite goals with clear outcomes
Tasks: Atomic, actionable items

3. When vs Deadline: Intention vs Obligation
When (Intention):

“I plan to work on this”
Flexible, low pressure
Can reschedule guilt-free

Deadline (Obligation):

“This must be done by”
Fixed, high pressure
Use sparingly

4. Status Simplicity
Tasks/Projects: open | completed | canceled
Areas: No status (always active)
Why: Reduces decision fatigue, clear semantics
5. Inbox → Organize → Schedule

Capture: Quick entry, minimal friction
Organize: Assign to project/area
Schedule: Set when/deadline when ready

6. Recurring Tasks
Fixed Schedule: Team standup every Monday
After Completion: Change air filter 3 months after completing
7. Tags: Light Categorization
Tags enhance, don’t define organization. Primary organization comes from Areas and Projects.
What Personal OS Keeps

Areas → Projects → Tasks hierarchy
When vs Deadline semantics
Simple status model
Inbox → Organize → Schedule workflow
Tag-based enhancement

What Personal OS Adds

Backlog App: Lower commitment capture
Markdown Storage: Git-trackable, future-proof
AI Integration: Natural language parsing
ULID Identifiers: Globally unique, sortable
ISO 8601 Everywhere: Standards-based formats

Best Practices

Start Simple: Use only required properties initially
Review Regularly: Daily (Today), Weekly (Projects), Monthly (Areas)
Use Deadlines Sparingly: Preserves meaning
Keep Projects Focused: 10-15 active max
Make Tasks Actionable: Start with verbs

App Schemas - Technical specifications
Development Standards - Naming conventions

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Projects and Areas Schema Analysis
Comparison of current implementation with Things 3 model and recommendations for schema updates.
Key Recommendations
Areas

REMOVE: status property (areas are perpetually active)
KEEP: uid, user, type, title, icon, sort-order, description, tags, created-at

Projects

RENAME: status: active → status: open
REMOVE: planning status value
ADD: project-type: finite | ongoing
ADD: completed-at and canceled-at timestamps
Status values: open | completed | canceled

Tasks

RENAME: not-started | in-progress → open
RENAME: cancelled → canceled
ADD: completed-at and canceled-at timestamps
ENHANCE: repeat property (after-completion patterns)
Status values: open | completed | canceled

Things 3 vs Current Implementation
What We’re Doing Better

Explicit priority property (p0-p3)
Time estimates (ISO 8601 durations)
Separate description from notes
ULID tracking
Rich timestamps

What Things 3 Does Better (Adopted)

Areas without status (perpetual)
Project types (finite vs ongoing)
Completion date tracking
Simpler status model
After-completion recurrence

Status Model Alignment
Things 3 Model:

Open: Active, default state
Completed: Successfully finished
Canceled: Dismissed without completion

Rationale: 15 years proved this works. Distinguishing “not-started” from “in-progress” adds unnecessary complexity.
Project Types

Finite: Clear end date and deliverable (most projects)
Ongoing: Perpetual container for recurring work

When vs Deadline
When: “I plan to work on this” (flexible)
Deadline: “This must be done by” (fixed)
Most tasks use when OR neither. Deadlines used sparingly.

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Template Engine
Simple template variable substitution system for creating files from templates.
Overview
The template engine provides {{variable}} syntax for automatic content generation with support for ULID generation, timestamps, user context, and custom variables.
Features

Simple syntax: {{variable}} placeholders
Auto-generation: UIDs, timestamps, dates automatically populated
Custom variables: Pass any custom data
YAML support: Properly formats lists and objects
CLI and library: Use from command line or Python code

Quick Start
Command Line
python3 lib/template_engine.py templates/backlog-template.md '{"title": "My Task", "priority": "1"}'
Python
from lib.template_engine import render_template
 
variables = {
    'title': 'Implement feature X',
    'user': 'tomboo',
    'priority': 'p1',
    'tags': ['feature', 'framework']
}
 
content = render_template('templates/backlog-template.md', variables)
Auto-Generated Variables

Common: user, title, type, tags, status
Backlog: priority, category, estimate, description, context

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Natural Language Parser
Extract structured data from conversational descriptions for backlog items.
Overview
The NLP parser enables frictionless capture by accepting natural language descriptions and automatically extracting structured metadata.
Features

Date parsing: Relative (tomorrow, next week) and absolute (Jan 15, 2025-01-15)
Priority extraction: Maps keywords to codes (critical → p0, high → p1)
Estimate parsing: Converts time expressions to ISO 8601 (2h → P2H, 30m → PT30M)
Category detection: @category syntax
Tag extraction: tag syntax
Title cleaning: Removes parsed tokens

Quick Start
Command Line
python3 lib/nlp_parser.py "research Obsidian API tomorrow @learning #technical high 2h"
# Output: {date: "2025-12-16", priority: "1", estimate: "P2H", category: "learning", tags: ["technical"], title: "Research Obsidian API"}
Python
from lib.nlp_parser import parse_backlog_input
 
result = parse_backlog_input("fix critical bug in auth system p0 30m @technical")
# {priority: 'p0', estimate: 'PT30M', category: 'technical', title: 'Fix bug in auth system'}
Date Parsing
Relative: tomorrow, today, next week, next month, in 3 days
Day names: next Monday, next Friday
Absolute: Jan 15, 2025-12-31, 12/31
Priority Mapping

























KeywordsCodecritical, urgent, p0p0high, important, p1p1medium, normal, p2p2low, p3p3
Estimate Parsing

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.title: Link Manager
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Link Manager
Programmatic access to UID registry and wikilink management for the vault.
Philosophy
Work WITH Obsidian, not against it:

Obsidian handles interactive editing (renames auto-update links)
LinkManager handles programmatic operations (AI, scripts, healing)
Together they create a robust system

Core Concepts
UID Registry

Location: .obsidian/uid-registry.json (git-ignored)
Purpose: Fast UID → file path lookup
Generation: On-demand via health checks
Format: {"UID": "path/to/file.md"}

Wikilink Formats
[[file-name]]                          # Shortest path
[[folder/file-name]]                   # Relative path
[[file-name|Display Text]]             # With display name
[[../projects/project-001|Project]]    # Relative from source
Usage Examples
Basic Setup
from lib.link_manager import LinkManager
lm = LinkManager('/path/to/vault')
lm.load_registry()
Creating Links from UIDs
projects = lm.find_by_title("Website Redesign", type_filter="project")
if projects:
    link = lm.create_wikilink(
        uid=projects[0]['uid'],
        from_file="database/tasks/task-009.md",
        display="Website Redesign"
    )
    # Returns: "[[../projects/project-001|Website Redesign]]"
Checking for Broken Links
broken = lm.find_broken_links("planning/backlog/backlog-001.md")
for prop_name, broken_link in broken:
    print(f"Broken: {prop_name}: {broken_link}")
Healing Broken Links
healed = lm.heal_broken_link(broken_link, source_file)
Key Methods

load_registry() - Load or rebuild registry
find_by_title() - Search by title with optional type filter
create_wikilink() - Create wikilink from UID
find_broken_links() - Check file for broken links
heal_broken_link() - Attempt to heal via UID lookup

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.title: Backlog Review Workflow
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDF.content:
Backlog Review Workflow
A structured approach to managing the backlog inbox, ensuring ideas don’t get lost while maintaining focus on current priorities.
Philosophy
The backlog serves as a capture inbox - a place to quickly dump ideas, tasks, and reminders without breaking focus. But an inbox only works if it’s regularly processed.
Review Cadence
Daily Review (5 minutes)
When: Morning, before starting focused work
Steps:

Open backlog view in Obsidian
Scan items added since last review
For each new item, ask: “Is this urgent or time-sensitive?”

Urgent? → Convert to task with when: today
Time-sensitive? → Add deadline property
Neither? → Leave for weekly review



Anti-patterns:

Don’t triage everything (that’s weekly review)
Don’t spend more than 5 minutes
Don’t reorganize or categorize

Weekly Review (30 minutes)
When: Friday afternoon or Sunday evening
Steps:

Review (10 min) - Sort by date (oldest first), read all not-started items
Prioritize (5 min) - Adjust priorities based on current goals
Categorize (5 min) - Ensure items have appropriate category/tags
Prune (5 min) - Mark stale items as cancelled or delete
Promote (5 min) - Convert high-value items to tasks

Questions to ask:

Does this still matter to me?
If I could only do 3 things from this list, which would they be?
Is this a task, a project, or just a someday/maybe idea?

Status Transitions

























StatusUse when…not-startedNew item, not yet triagedsomedayGood idea, but not actionable in next 1-2 monthscancelledNo longer relevant or decided againstcompletedItem done directly without becoming a task
Backlog → Task Promotion

Create new task in _database/database-core/tasks-table/
Copy relevant content from backlog item
Set task properties: when, project/area, estimate
Update backlog item: status: completed or delete

Tips

Daily: Set a 5-minute timer, stop when it rings
Weekly: Same time each week, quiet environment
Be ruthless: If untouched for 4+ weeks, seriously reconsider
Use someday liberally: Deferring with intention is not giving up

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDM.title: Migration Guide
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KDM.content:
Migration Guide
This document explains how to deploy the Personal Operating System framework to a new Obsidian vault.
Prerequisites

Python 3.9+ installed
Obsidian vault initialized
Git for version control (recommended)

Step 1: Install Python Dependencies
pip install pyyaml ulid-py jsonschema
Verify installation:
python3 -c "import yaml, ulid, jsonschema; print('Dependencies OK')"
Step 2: Copy Framework Files
Copy these directories from the source vault to your target vault:
# From source vault root
cp -r _framework/ /path/to/target-vault/
cp -r .claude/commands/ /path/to/target-vault/.claude/commands/
Step 3: Create Backend Structure
Create the database directory structure:
mkdir -p _database/database-core
Create _database/database-core/schema.json with your type definitions. Start with a minimal schema:
{
  "$schema": "json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "database-core-schema",
  "title": "Core Database Schema",
  "type": "object",
 
  "$defs": {
    "uid": {
      "type": "string",
      "pattern": "^[0-9A-HJKMNP-TV-Z]{26}$",
      "description": "26-character ULID"
    },
    "iso-date": {
      "type": "string",
      "pattern": "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$"
    }
  },
 
  "properties": {
    "uid": { "$ref": "#/$defs/uid" },
    "type": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["session", "note", "task"]
    },
    "date": { "$ref": "#/$defs/iso-date" },
    "user": { "type": "string" }
  },
 
  "required": ["uid", "type"]
}
Step 4: Create Tables
Create table directories for each entity type:
mkdir -p _database/database-core/sessions-table
mkdir -p _database/database-core/notes-table
# Add more as needed
Step 5: Create vault.json (Optional)
Create vault.json in your vault root for multi-database configurations:
{
  "name": "my-vault",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "My Personal OS vault",
  "framework": "personal-os-framework",
  "framework_version": "1.0.0",
  "databases": {
    "core": "_database/database-core"
  }
}
Step 6: Configure CLAUDE.md
Create or update CLAUDE.md in your vault root with:

Vault overview and structure
Session workflow commands (/session-start, /session-end, etc.)
App-specific instructions
Git workflow guidelines

See the reference vault’s CLAUDE.md for a complete example.
Step 7: Validate Installation
Run health check to verify everything is working:
cd /path/to/vault
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py
Expected output for a new vault:
Vault Health Check
==================
Database: core
  Tables checked: 2
  Files validated: 0
  Issues found: 0

Overall: HEALTHY

Step 8: Create First Items
Test by creating items with proper frontmatter:
Session note (_database/database-core/sessions-table/session-20251228-001.md):
---
session: 1
user: yourname
type: session
focus: [setup, migration]
duration-estimate: ~1h
created-at: 2025-12-28T10:00:00-08:00
---
 
# Session 2025-12-28-1: Initial Setup
 
## Summary
First session in the new vault.
Migration Checklist

 Python dependencies installed (pyyaml, ulid-py, jsonschema)
 _framework/ copied to vault root
 .claude/commands/ copied (if using Claude Code)
 _database/database-core/ created with schema.json
 Table directories created
 vault.json created (optional)
 CLAUDE.md configured
 Health check passes
 First session note created and validates

Adding Additional Databases
For creative writing or specialized content, add separate databases:
mkdir -p _database/database-studio
Create _database/database-studio/schema.json with type-specific definitions:
{
  "$schema": "json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "database-studio-schema",
  "title": "Studio Database Schema",
  "type": "object",
 
  "properties": {
    "type": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["beat", "character", "location", "scene"]
    }
  }
}
Update vault.json:
{
  "databases": {
    "core": "_database/database-core",
    "studio": "_database/database-studio"
  }
}

Troubleshooting
Common Issues
“ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘yaml’”
pip install pyyaml
“ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘ulid’”
pip install ulid-py
Health check fails with “Invalid ULID”

ULIDs must be exactly 26 characters, uppercase Crockford Base32
Generate valid ULIDs: python3 -c "from ulid import ULID; print(ULID())"
Invalid characters: I, L, O, U are not used in Crockford Base32

Health check fails with “Missing type property”

Every file in a table must have a type: property in frontmatter
The type must match one of the values in your schema’s type.enum
Run python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py --fix to auto-add missing types

Schema validation errors

Check that property values match the schema patterns
Dates must be YYYY-MM-DD format
Timestamps must be ISO 8601 with timezone (e.g., 2025-12-28T10:00:00-08:00)
Tags must be arrays: tags: [tag1, tag2] not tags: tag1, tag2

Obsidian doesn’t see frontmatter changes

Frontmatter must start on line 1 with ---
Close with --- on its own line
No blank lines before opening ---
Restart Obsidian or re-open the file to refresh

Git conflicts in session notes

Always run /session-start at the beginning of work
Use /session-commit for periodic checkpoints
Never edit the same vault from multiple machines simultaneously

Validation Commands
# Check overall vault health
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py
 
# Check specific database
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py --database core
 
# Auto-fix common issues
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py --fix
 
# Validate single file
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py --file path/to/file.md
 
# Run test suite
./_framework/scripts/run-tests.sh
Getting Help

Check the docs library: _database/database-docs/docs-table/
Review CLAUDE.md for workflow instructions
Run /health-check for automated diagnostics

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KEJ.title: Beads Evaluation
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KEJ.content:
Beads Evaluation
Evaluation of Beads as a persistent memory system for AI coding agents.
What is Beads?
Beads is a lightweight memory system for AI coding agents that replaces ephemeral in-context task lists with a persistent, Git-backed issue tracker.
Author: Steve Yegge
Repository: github.com/steveyegge/beads
Video: youtu.be/cWBVMEHPgQU
Documentation

GitHub README
MCP Integration
Intro Article (Medium)
Better Stack Guide

Installation
# Homebrew (macOS)
brew install steveyegge/beads/bd
 
# npm
npm install -g @beads/bd
 
# Go
go install github.com/steveyegge/beads/cmd/bd@latest
Core Problem Beads Solves
AI agent to-do lists are fundamentally broken:

Only exist inside a single session
Can’t be shared, versioned, or trusted long-term
Markdown workarounds drift, bloat context, and break agent alignment

Beads moves task state outside the LLM context window.
How It Works
Storage

SQLite database - Local, fast access
JSONL file - Committed to Git for sharing and history
Git hooks - Keep memory in sync across pulls/pushes

Key Features





























FeatureDescriptionDependenciesTasks can block or depend on other tasksPrioritiesStandard priority levelsAssignmentsMulti-developer supportEpicsGroup related issuesReady querybd ready shows tasks with no blockers
CLI Commands
bd init          # Initialize Beads in repo
bd create        # Create new task
bd list          # List all tasks
bd ready         # Show tasks with no blockers
bd onboard       # Update agent instruction files
bd doctor        # Fix configuration issues
Agent Onboarding
bd onboard updates agent instruction files (like CLAUDE.md) to tell agents:

Don’t use internal to-do lists
Don’t create markdown task files
Use Beads for ALL task tracking

Sentry Integration
Pull production errors from Sentry and auto-create Beads tasks with:

Error URLs
Stack traces
Root-cause analysis (via Sentry Seer AI)

Evaluation for Our System
Strengths

Persistent agent memory - Tasks survive context resets
Git-friendly - JSONL merges cleanly, no bracket conflicts
Dependencies - First-class blocks/depends-on relationships
Agent-queryable - CLI designed for agent interaction
Multi-agent support - Multiple agents can share task state

Weaknesses (for our use case)

Different workflow model - Designed for autonomous agents, not collaborative sessions
Not Obsidian-native - Can’t wiki-link, no Bases views, no daily note integration
Duplicate systems - Would have tasks in two places
Overhead - Another tool to install and maintain
Overkill - Our sessions are 1-2 hours with user present

Recommendation
Don’t add Beads directly. Instead, adopt its best ideas natively:

























Beads FeatureNative ImplementationTask dependenciesAdd blocks/depends-on to task schemaReady queryCreate “Ready to Work” Bases viewAgent instructionsAlready have CLAUDE.mdGit-friendly storageAlready using markdown + git
When Beads Would Make Sense

Long autonomous agent runs (hours/days)
Multi-agent collaboration on same codebase
Codebases without existing task management
Projects where Obsidian isn’t the primary tool

Ideas to Adopt
Task Dependencies
Add to task schema:
blocks:
  - "[[01KCPDVSE76W53TN7NQAMV0KDT]]"
depends-on:
  - "[[01KCPDVSDTMNNXHH8KHRW1EEHT]]"
Agent-Ready Query
Create Bases view filtering:

status: open
No items in depends-on that are open
Sorted by priority

Automatic Task Creation
Convert tool output (test failures, health check issues) into backlog items automatically.
Landing Checklist
Per-task completion checklist (not just session-level):

Run relevant tests
Verify changes
Update documentation if needed

Related

Beads - Tool overview note
How to Give Your AI Agent Long-Term Memory - Video summary
01KEJCZAW595XJPNGPFQ5JZS85 - Backlog item for dependencies feature
