_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KF0.content:
YouTube Queue App PRD
Version: 0.1 (Draft)
Author: tomboo
Vision
A personal YouTube queue management system that brings intentional video consumption into the Personal Operating System framework. Instead of mindlessly browsing YouTube’s algorithm-driven recommendations, this app enables saving, categorizing, prioritizing, and tracking video content with rich metadata and note-taking capabilities.
Problem Statement
YouTube consumption is often reactive and algorithm-driven:

Videos get lost in “Watch Later” lists with no prioritization
No way to categorize by learning goals, projects, or interests
Difficult to take notes or track insights from videos
No visibility into what content is most valuable to consume next
Missing context when returning to saved videos weeks later

Goals

Intentional Consumption - Transform passive browsing into deliberate learning and entertainment
Priority-Based Queue - Always know what to watch next based on your priorities
Rich Context - Auto-fetch metadata, transcripts, and chapters for informed decisions
Knowledge Capture - Take notes and track insights from watched content
Framework Integration - Seamless fit with existing Personal OS patterns and workflows

Non-Goals

Building a YouTube client or player
Downloading video files (only metadata/transcripts)
Social features or sharing
Automated recommendation engine
Mobile app (Obsidian desktop is primary interface)

Core Features
1. Queue Item Management
Create queue items from YouTube URLs:

Paste YouTube share URL during any session
Natural language: “add to youtube queue youtube.com/watch…”
Extract video ID, store URL
Set initial priority and category

Queue item properties:

Standard framework properties (uid, date, user, status, priority, tags)
url - YouTube video URL
video-id - Extracted YouTube video ID
title - Video title (auto-fetched)
channel - Channel name (auto-fetched)
duration - Video duration (auto-fetched)
category - Content category (learning, entertainment, research, etc.)
watched-at - Timestamp when watched
rating - Personal rating after watching (1-5)
notes - Free-form notes about the video

2. Content Storage System
General-purpose _database/content-storage/ system:

Stores fetched metadata, transcripts, and chapters
Combined single-file format per video
Lazy loading: fetch when status changes to “watching”
Reusable by future apps (podcasts, articles, etc.)

Content file structure:
_database/content-storage/youtube/{video-id}.md

Content file contains:

Video metadata (title, channel, duration, upload date, description)
Chapter markers (if available)
Full transcript (if available)
Thumbnail URL

3. Priority-Based Queue Views
Standard Bases views:

Watch Next - Unwatched items sorted by priority (p0 first)
By Category - Items grouped by category
Recently Watched - Completed items with notes
All Items - Complete list with filtering

4. Watching Workflow
Status progression:

queued - Initial state, in watch list
watching - Currently watching (triggers content fetch)
watched - Completed viewing
abandoned - Started but won’t finish

On status change to “watching”:

Auto-fetch content via yt-dlp (if not already cached)
Store in content-storage
User can reference transcript/chapters while watching

5. Natural Language Creation
Support conversational item creation:
add youtube video youtu.be/abc123 @learning high
queue this video youtube.com/watch @entertainment p3

Parse:

URL (required)
Category via @ prefix
Priority via p0-p3 or high/medium/low
Tags via # prefix

Development Phases
Phase 1: Core Queue Management
Goal: Basic queue functionality without metadata fetching
Deliverables:

YouTube app directory structure (README, schema, views)
Queue item creation from URLs
Manual property entry (title, channel, duration)
Standard Bases views (Watch Next, By Category, All Items)
Status workflow (queued → watching → watched)
Natural language creation support

Value: Immediate utility for tracking YouTube queue with prioritization
Dependencies: None (builds on existing framework)
Phase 2: Content Storage Infrastructure
Goal: Establish general-purpose content storage system
Deliverables:

_database/content-storage/ directory structure
Content storage schema and conventions
YouTube content file format specification
Manual content file creation capability
Link queue items to content files

Value: Foundation for rich content without external dependencies
Dependencies: Phase 1
Phase 3: Automated Metadata Fetching
Goal: Auto-populate content via yt-dlp
Deliverables:

yt-dlp integration for metadata extraction
Lazy fetch on status change to “watching”
Auto-populate queue item title/channel/duration
Store full content (metadata, chapters, transcript) in content-storage
Error handling for unavailable content

Value: Zero-friction content enrichment, searchable transcripts
Dependencies: Phase 2, yt-dlp installed on system
Phase 4: Enhanced Workflows
Goal: Polish and productivity features
Deliverables:

Rating system after watching
Notes integration with timestamp references
“Quick add” slash command
Dashboard view with queue statistics
Health checks for orphaned content files

Value: Complete knowledge capture workflow
Dependencies: Phase 3
Phase 5: Future Expansion (Conceptual)
Goal: Extend patterns to other content types
Potential:

Podcast queue (same patterns, different fetcher)
Article/webpage queue (readability extraction)
Unified “Content Queue” app
Cross-content search

Dependencies: Phase 4 proven successful
Content Storage Design
Philosophy
The content storage system is designed as a general-purpose cache for external content metadata. Key principles:

Separation of Concerns - Queue items (what to watch) are separate from content files (reference material)
Content-Addressed Storage - Files named by content ID, not date
Lazy Loading - Fetch only when needed, not on queue creation
Idempotent - Re-fetching overwrites existing content safely
Reusable - Same patterns work for YouTube, podcasts, articles

Directory Structure
_database/content-storage/
  youtube/
    {video-id}.md       # Combined metadata + transcript + chapters
  podcasts/             # Future
  articles/             # Future

Content File Schema
---
content-type: youtube
content-id: dQw4w9WgXcQ
url: youtube.com/watch
fetched-at: 2025-12-24T10:00:00-08:00
title: "Video Title Here"
channel: "Channel Name"
channel-url: youtube.com/@channel
duration: "3:32"
upload-date: 2024-01-15
view-count: 1234567
thumbnail: i.ytimg.com/vi/dQw4w9WgXcQ/maxresdefault.jpg
---
 
# Video Title Here
 
## Description
 
[Video description from YouTube]
 
## Chapters
 
- 0:00 Introduction
- 1:30 Main Topic
- 2:45 Conclusion
 
## Transcript
 
[Full transcript if available]
Queue Item to Content Link
Queue items reference content via video-id:
video-id: dQw4w9WgXcQ
content-file: "[[../../content-storage/youtube/dQw4w9WgXcQ]]"
Success Criteria
Phase 1 Success

Can create queue items from YouTube URLs
Can view prioritized watch queue in Bases
Can update status through watching workflow
Natural language creation works

Phase 2 Success

Content storage structure established
Content files can be created and linked
Pattern documented for reuse

Phase 3 Success

yt-dlp successfully extracts metadata
Lazy fetch triggers on “watching” status
Transcripts searchable in Obsidian

Overall Success

YouTube consumption feels intentional, not reactive
Can easily find “what should I watch next” based on priorities
Notes and insights captured and searchable
Framework health checks validate YouTube app items

Technical Dependencies
Required

Obsidian with Bases plugin (existing)
Personal OS framework (existing)

Phase 3+ Requirements

yt-dlp - Command-line tool for YouTube metadata/transcript extraction
Python 3.x - For running yt-dlp and processing output
Internet connection - For fetching content

yt-dlp Capabilities

# Transcript extraction
yt-dlp --write-auto-sub --sub-lang en --skip-download "URL"
 
# Chapter extraction (in JSON metadata)
yt-dlp --dump-json "URL" | jq '.chapters'
Open Questions

Offline handling - What happens if yt-dlp fails (video removed, network issues)?
Transcript languages - Support multiple languages or English-only?
Content updates - Re-fetch if video metadata changes?
Bulk import - Import existing “Watch Later” playlist?
Privacy - Any concerns with storing YouTube data locally?

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KF0.title: Architectural Review - Personal Operating System Framework
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KF0.content:
Architectural Review - Personal Operating System Framework
Version: 1.0
Reviewer: Senior Dev/Architect
Review Date: 2026-01-15
Framework Version: 1.0.0
Executive Summary
The Personal Operating System framework implements a flat-file database architecture using Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, validated against JSON Schema, and organized via the Obsidian Bases plugin. This review evaluates design decisions, identifies architectural issues, and provides recommendations.
Overall Assessment: The architecture is well-designed for its scope (single-user PKM with ~500 files) but has several consistency issues and scalability concerns that should be addressed to ensure long-term maintainability.








































AspectRatingNotesDesign CoherenceB+Strong separation of concerns, minor duplicationSchema DesignBComprehensive but monolithic, needs refactoringConsistencyC+Mixed patterns, naming inconsistenciesScalabilityB-Adequate for current scale, ceiling visiblePerformanceB+Fast reads, validation overhead acceptableMaintainabilityBGood tooling, documentation gaps
Architecture Overview
System Architecture
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    OBSIDIAN (UI Layer)                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │              Bases Plugin (Views/Query)              │   │
│  └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘   │
└───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┘
            │
┌───────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           │           CLAUDE CODE (AI Layer)                │
│  ┌────────▼─────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Slash Commands   │  │  Session Workflows              │   │
│  │ (/session-*)     │  │  (start, commit, end)           │   │
│  └──────────────────┘  └────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
┌───────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           │         FRAMEWORK (Logic Layer)                 │
│  ┌────────▼─────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Python Libs     │  │  JSON Schema Validation         │   │
│  │  - validators    │  │  - database-core/schema.json    │   │
│  │  - template_eng  │  │  - database-docs/schema.json    │   │
│  │  - nlp_parser    │  │  - database-studio/schema.json  │   │
│  │  - link_manager  │  │                                 │   │
│  └──────────────────┘  └────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
┌───────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           │          DATA LAYER (Flat-File DB)              │
│  ┌────────▼──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              _database/                               │  │
│  │  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐  │  │
│  │  │  database-core  │ │  database-docs  │ │ studio  │  │  │
│  │  │  ├─tasks-table  │ │  └─docs-table   │ │ (beats, │  │  │
│  │  │  ├─sessions-*   │ │                 │ │  chars, │  │  │
│  │  │  ├─backlog-*    │ │                 │ │  locs)  │  │  │
│  │  │  └─...          │ │                 │ │         │  │  │
│  │  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────┘  │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
┌───────────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     GIT (Version Control)                   │
│        Tracked markdown, committed at session boundaries    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Current Scale



































DatabaseTablesFilesPurposedatabase-core9278Operational data (tasks, sessions, backlog)database-docs123Framework documentationdatabase-studio3122Creative writing metadataTotal13423
Key Design Decisions

Flat-file over relational database - Git-friendly, portable, human-readable
JSON Schema validation - Type safety without compilation
ULID identifiers - Chronologically sortable, globally unique
Markdown + YAML frontmatter - Standard format, tool ecosystem
Bases plugin for views - Query interface without custom code


Design Analysis
Strengths
1. Separation of Concerns
The architecture cleanly separates:

Data (_database/) from Logic (_framework/) from Views (components/)
Schema definitions (JSON) from templates (Markdown) from validation (Python)

This enables independent evolution of each layer.
2. Schema-Driven Validation
Using JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) provides:

Declarative type definitions
IDE autocomplete potential
Language-agnostic validation
Self-documenting constraints

The conditional schema pattern (allOf with if/then) elegantly handles type-specific properties.
3. ULID Identifier System
ULIDs provide significant advantages over UUIDs or auto-increment:

Chronological sorting without date fields
128-bit uniqueness (collision-resistant)
Human-readable (26 chars vs 36 for UUID)
No central authority needed

4. Git-Centric Workflow
Session-based commits with meaningful messages create:

Full audit trail
Easy rollback capabilities
Offline-first operation
Natural backup via remote

5. AI-Native Design
The CLAUDE.md + slash commands pattern enables:

Contextual AI assistance
Consistent workflows
Natural language interaction
Schema-aware operations

Weaknesses
1. Monolithic Core Schema (533 lines)
The database-core/schema.json handles 9 entity types in one file using conditional logic. This creates:

Cognitive load (hard to understand full schema)
Merge conflicts on concurrent edits
Difficulty testing individual types
Unclear property ownership

Current pattern:
{
  "allOf": [
    { "if": { "properties": { "type": { "const": "task" } } },
      "then": { /* 50+ lines of task-specific schema */ } },
    { "if": { "properties": { "type": { "const": "session" } } },
      "then": { /* 40+ lines of session-specific schema */ } },
    // ... 7 more type definitions
  ]
}
2. Dual View System (Inconsistent)
Two parallel view systems exist:

_database/*/*/_index.base - Simple table views
components/*/*.base - Rich multi-view files

This creates confusion about where views live and maintains two sets of column configurations.
3. Status Value Inconsistency
Different entity types use incompatible status values:





























EntityStatus ValuesTaskopen, completed, canceledBacklognot-started, in-progress, open, completed, canceled, somedayProjectopen, completed, canceledNotedraft, active, archived, deprecatedSubscriptionactive, paused, cancelled, trial
This prevents unified status queries and complicates UI.
4. Timestamp Format Inconsistency
Files show inconsistent created-at formats:
# Some files:
created-at: 2026-01-09T10:00:00-08:00  # Full ISO with timezone
 
# Other files:
created-at: 2026-01-09T00:00:00        # Missing timezone
The schema accepts both, but this creates sorting issues and data quality concerns.
5. Missing Required Properties
Several files lack properties marked as required in documentation:

Tasks missing date property (schema allows it but docs require it)
Sessions missing actual-duration (optional but valuable)
Inconsistent description vs synopsis usage

6. Documentation Path Drift
README files reference non-existent paths:

standards/schemas/app-schemas.md (doesn’t exist)
standards/development.md (doesn’t exist)
APPS.md (doesn’t exist)

The migration to _database/database-docs/ is incomplete.

Scalability Analysis
Current Performance Profile









































OperationComplexityAt 500 FilesAt 5,000 FilesFile readO(1)<1ms<1msFull validationO(n)~2s~20sBases queryO(n)<100ms~1sULID uniqueness checkO(n)<100ms~1sLink integrity checkO(n*m)~500ms~50s
Scalability Ceiling
The architecture will encounter friction at these thresholds:
1,000+ files: Health check takes >5 seconds
5,000+ files: Bases queries become sluggish
10,000+ files: Git operations slow significantly
50,000+ files: Single-vault Obsidian performance degrades
Mitigation Strategies
For growth beyond current scale:

Index files - Pre-compute frequently-queried data
Database sharding - Split by date (archive old data)
Incremental validation - Only validate changed files
SQLite cache - Like MarkdownDB or Beads patterns


Consistency Analysis
Naming Conventions









































PatternExpectedActual ExamplesStatusTable directories{type}-tabletasks-table, sessions-tableCONSISTENTFile naming{type}-NNN.mdtask-127.md, backlog-056.mdMOSTLYPropertieskebab-casecreated-at, completed-atCONSISTENTProperty valueskebab-casenot-started, in-progressCONSISTENTTagskebab-caseframework, task-managementMOSTLY
File Naming Inconsistency
# Pattern 1: Sequential numbering
task-127.md, backlog-056.md, note-005.md

# Pattern 2: Date-based
session-20260109-001.md

# Pattern 3: Named files
area-personal.md, area-work.md

The mixed patterns complicate automation and sorting.
Schema Definition Locations

























TypeSchema LocationView LocationTasksdatabase-core/schema.jsoncomponents/project-management/tasks-base.baseDocsdatabase-docs/schema.jsoncomponents/docs/docs-base.baseSessionsdatabase-core/schema.jsoncomponents/sessions/sessions-base.base
The 1:1 mapping between schemas and databases is good, but README documentation doesn’t always match schema definitions.

Comparison to Industry Models
Similar Architectures
1. Flat-File CMS (Grav, Pico, Kirby)
Similarities:

Markdown + YAML frontmatter
File-based storage
Git-friendly

Differences:

This framework has stronger schema validation
AI-native workflows are unique
Session-based git workflow is novel

2. Static Site Generators (Jekyll, Hugo, 11ty)
Similarities:

Frontmatter-driven metadata
Build-time processing
Template systems

Differences:

SSGs optimize for HTML output; this optimizes for data management
This has runtime validation; SSGs validate at build time

3. Notion/Coda Database Pattern
Similarities:

Structured data with views
Property-based organization
Relational linking

Differences:

This is local-first; Notion is cloud-first
Git version control vs proprietary history
Open format vs vendor lock-in

4. MarkdownDB / Beads
Similarities:

Markdown as source of truth
Structured queries over files
Developer-focused

Differences:

MarkdownDB uses SQLite index; this uses Bases plugin
Beads targets autonomous agents; this targets human-AI collaboration

Recommended Model: Content-Layer Pattern
The closest industry standard is the Content Layer pattern used in modern JAMstack:
Source Files (Markdown)
    ↓ [Schema Definition]
Validated Content
    ↓ [Type-Safe API]
Application Code

This framework implements this pattern with:

Source: _database/*/*/*.md
Schema: schema.json files
API: Python validators + Bases queries


Key Issues & Recommendations
Critical Issues
Issue 1: Monolithic Schema
Problem: Single 533-line schema file handles 9 entity types
Impact: Maintenance burden, merge conflicts, cognitive load
Recommendation: Split into per-type schema files with $ref composition
// database-core/schemas/task.schema.json
{
  "$id": "task-schema",
  "allOf": [
    { "$ref": "common.schema.json" },
    { "properties": { "when": {...}, "deadline": {...} } }
  ]
}
Issue 2: Status Value Fragmentation
Problem: 5+ different status enums across entity types
Impact: No unified status queries, confusing UI
Recommendation: Define 2-3 status archetypes in common schema
// Proposed unified statuses
"status-lifecycle": ["pending", "active", "completed", "canceled"],
"status-content": ["draft", "active", "archived"]
Issue 3: Timestamp Timezone Inconsistency
Problem: created-at values mix timezone-aware and naive formats
Impact: Sorting errors, validation gaps
Recommendation: Enforce timezone in schema pattern, add migration script
High Priority
Issue 4: Documentation Path References
Problem: READMEs reference non-existent files
Impact: Broken links, user confusion
Recommendation: Audit all READMEs, update paths to _database/database-docs/
Issue 5: Dual View System
Problem: _index.base and components/*.base serve overlapping purposes
Impact: Maintenance duplication, unclear source of truth
Recommendation: Standardize on _index.base for data views, reserve components/ for dashboards
Medium Priority
Issue 6: File Naming Patterns
Problem: Mixed sequential, date-based, and named patterns
Impact: Inconsistent automation, sorting issues
Recommendation: Standardize on {type}-{YYYYMMDD}-{NNN}.md for temporal data, {type}-{slug}.md for reference data
Issue 7: Missing Computed Properties
Problem: No way to define computed/derived properties
Impact: Manual updates for age, duration, status rollups
Recommendation: Define computed property patterns in Bases (already partially done with subscription formulas)
Low Priority
Issue 8: No Property Changelog
Problem: Schema changes aren’t tracked formally
Impact: Migration uncertainty
Recommendation: Add _framework/schemas/CHANGELOG.md
Issue 9: Test Coverage Gaps
Problem: Tests exist but coverage is unclear
Impact: Regression risk
Recommendation: Add coverage reporting to test suite

Recommended Architecture Evolution
Phase 1: Consistency (Immediate)

Fix timestamp formats - Add migration script for timezone normalization
Update README paths - Point to current doc locations
Consolidate view strategy - Document when to use _index.base vs components/

Phase 2: Schema Refactoring (Next Quarter)

Split monolithic schema into per-type files
Introduce common schema with shared definitions
Standardize status values across entity types
Add schema changelog for tracking evolution

Phase 3: Scalability Prep (As Needed)

Implement incremental validation - Only check changed files
Add SQLite index - For complex queries (like MarkdownDB)
Define archival strategy - Move old sessions/tasks to archive database
Consider multi-vault - If creative writing grows significantly


Conclusion
The Personal Operating System framework demonstrates solid architectural thinking with its flat-file database approach, JSON Schema validation, and AI-native workflows. The main areas requiring attention are:

Consistency - Unify status values, timestamps, and file naming
Schema organization - Split monolithic schema, add common definitions
Documentation - Update stale references, complete migration

The architecture is well-suited for its current scope (~500 files, single user) and can scale to ~5,000 files with minor optimizations. Beyond that threshold, consider SQLite indexing or multi-vault strategies.
Priority Actions:

Fix timestamp timezone inconsistency (data quality)
Update README documentation paths (user experience)
Plan schema refactoring (maintainability)

Related

Development Standards
Common Properties Schema
App-Specific Schemas
Migration Guide

References

Flat-File CMS Guide
MarkdownDB - Similar markdown-to-database pattern
Obsidian Vault Architecture
PKM System Design Best Practices


Comments
2026-01-15: Created
Comprehensive architectural review commissioned to evaluate framework design, identify issues, and recommend improvements. Analysis covers ~423 files across 3 databases.

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KF1.title: Framework v2 Architecture Plan
_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KF1.content:
our plan is solid, and (crucially) it matches a pattern that already exists in the wild: “Markdown as source of truth, generated SQLite index for fast query + validation + AI tooling.” You do not need to start from scratch.
High-level evaluation of your plan
What you’re proposing (as an architecture)


Source of truth: Markdown + YAML frontmatter (local-first, human-readable, Git-friendly)


Derived store: SQLite index (queryable, fast, can support FTS)


Index pipeline: parse → validate → emit DB → flag/fix issues


UI: Obsidian (editor, backlinks, graph, plugins)


AI integration: use the SQLite index + file paths as retrieval layer; optionally expose as MCP / local service


Versioning: Git


This is a very sane architecture. It scales better than “Obsidian-only metadata querying” because SQLite gives you:


stable queries


performance on large vaults


a clean interface for AI tools (RAG, semantic search, metadata filters)


deterministic validation/fixes


Key risk to manage
Don’t let SQLite become a competing source of truth. It must remain:


derived


rebuildable


throwaway


schema-controlled


If you keep that invariant, you get the best of both worlds.

Existing models you can reuse (so you don’t reinvent the wheel)
1) MarkdownDB (direct hit for “Markdown → SQLite index”)
MarkdownDB is essentially your “sqlite index generated from markdown” requirement, already packaged. It indexes markdown files (including frontmatter/tags) into SQLite. (GitHub)
How it helps you:


jump-start the index layer quickly


gives you a known DB schema pattern (files table + join tables like tags)


lets you focus your effort on validation + fixers + AI integration rather than basic indexing


Where you’ll likely extend it:


custom frontmatter schema enforcement


error reporting + auto-fix pipeline


Obsidian-specific concepts (wikilinks, vault-relative paths, attachments)


2) “Obsidian Index Service” pattern (watch vault → SQLite)
There’s an open-source pattern that does exactly what you described: monitor an Obsidian vault directory and index Markdown files—metadata and full content—into SQLite. (GitHub)
How it helps you:


shows a practical architecture for “continuous indexing”


good starting point if you want a daemon/service instead of a CLI rebuild


3) Dendron’s “indexing + schema-ish metadata” approach (conceptual model)
Dendron is markdown + frontmatter and has a strong “indexing server” concept in its ecosystem. It’s VS Code–based rather than Obsidian-based, but the architecture is relevant: local-first notes, generated indexes, and conventions/templates. (Dendron)
How it helps you:


conventions for required frontmatter


systematic “note type” approaches


operational patterns for large vaults


4) Obsidian plugin ecosystem (UI-side helpers)
Obsidian itself has a very active plugin ecosystem. You can reuse:


indexing helpers (even if not SQLite)


metadata maintenance patterns


AI plugins for in-editor workflows (Obsidian)


This won’t replace SQLite indexing, but it can reduce how much custom UI you build.

The “best reuse path” (what I’d recommend)
If your goal is a general-purpose, consistent base (framework, not content), the best path is:
Reuse for indexing, build for correctness + AI


Use MarkdownDB (or similar) for the base SQLite index (GitHub)


Add your framework layers:


Schema validation for frontmatter (JSON Schema or equivalent)


Error reporting (machine-readable report + human-friendly summary)


Optional auto-fix with “safe fixers” (timezone normalization, ULID format fix, missing defaults, etc.)


AI integration that reads from SQLite (filters + FTS + embeddings table if you want it)




This gets you to a working, maintainable system with minimal reinvention.

A concrete “framework target” (what “done” looks like)
Repo structure (suggested)


_vault/ (your Obsidian vault content — unchanged)


_framework/


schemas/ (frontmatter schemas by type)


indexer/ (parse → validate → sqlite)


fixers/ (optional auto-fixes)


reports/ (latest validation run results)


ai/ (RAG layer; MCP server optional)


cli/ (commands: index, validate, fix, report)




markdown.db (generated; in .gitignore)


CLI contracts


lexi index → rebuild sqlite


lexi validate → report errors, no modifications


lexi fix → apply safe fixes + produce a diff report


lexi doctor → “vault health” summary (counts, missing fields, broken links, etc.)


That’s the general-purpose base you can reuse forever.

Do you need Logseq DB mode or “database-first” tools?
Probably not. Logseq’s DB/SQLite mode trends toward a single database file as primary storage, which fights your requirement of Git-first markdown source-of-truth. Even Logseq community guidance often points to sticking with Markdown mode if you want Git/SyncThing workflows. (Logseq)
So: keep your plan. Don’t flip the storage model.

Bottom line


Your plan is strong.


You can reuse MarkdownDB as the indexing substrate (big acceleration). (GitHub)


You can reuse the “watch + index to sqlite” service pattern if you want continuous updates. (GitHub)


Your unique value is the validation + fixer pipeline + AI layer tuned for Obsidian + Git.


If you want, I’ll propose two concrete implementation tracks (simple CLI rebuild vs continuous daemon) and a minimal schema set that makes the framework general-purpose without being overdesigned.

This is a foundational decision, so I’ll be opinionated and explicit. The goal is: boring, predictable, refactor-safe, AI-friendly, Obsidian-friendly, Git-friendly.

1. File naming pattern
Recommendation: ULID-only filenames (with optional human alias in frontmatter)
Yes — use ULID as the filename.
Do not encode meaning in filenames.
Canonical filename
01JGFNLP8Z2XK4H7MZ9VYQ8C4A.md

Why this is the right choice


Rename-proof: titles, semantics, hierarchy can change freely


Stable identifiers across refactors, moves, and merges


Git-friendly: diffs remain clean; moves don’t break links


AI-friendly: ULID is a perfect primary key


Obsidian-safe: works fine with wikilinks


How humans navigate instead


title frontmatter (primary)


aliases frontmatter


folder structure (high-level grouping only)


Obsidian search, backlinks, Bases, SQLite queries



Filenames are for machines. Titles are for humans.


What not to do
Avoid:


2026-01-15-my-thoughts.md


task-fix-schema.md


note-xyz.md


mixed patterns (doc-024.md, task-127.md, etc.)


Those create long-term entropy.

One exception (optional)
You may allow:
01JGFNLP8Z2XK4H7MZ9VYQ8C4A--schema-design.md

…but only if:


ULID is first


everything after -- is non-canonical and disposable


your tooling ignores suffixes completely


If you don’t need this, skip it.

2. Linking rule (critical)
Always link by filename ULID, never by title:
See [[01JGFNLP8Z2XK4H7MZ9VYQ8C4A]]
Your indexer can optionally support title-based backlinks for convenience, but ULID must be the ground truth.

3. Standard core frontmatter (minimal, universal)
This is the non-negotiable core. Every file has these.
type: note
title: Human-readable title
status: active
created-at: 2026-01-15T08:42:31Z
Field-by-field rationale
uid


Must match filename ULID exactly


Enforced by validator


Never changes


type
Controls schema, views, behavior.
Examples:
note | doc | task | project | person | asset | session | backlog

Use a small, closed set. New types require a schema file.
title


Human-readable


Can change freely


Used in Obsidian UI, Bases, AI summaries


status
Lifecycle state (normalized per type but same field everywhere):
draft | active | on-hold | completed | deprecated | archived

Avoid ad-hoc statuses.
created-at


ISO 8601


Timezone required


Immutable once set (except fixer repair)



4. Strongly recommended (but optional) core fields
These are extremely high-value and worth standardizing early.
aliases:
  - Alternate title
  - Old name
 
tags:
  - concept
  - planning
 
source:
  kind: manual
  ref: null
aliases


Enables human-friendly wikilinks


Preserves continuity across renames


Your indexer can auto-backfill aliases when titles change


tags


Flat, lowercase


Avoid hierarchical tags (a/b/c)


Use links for structure, tags for facets


source
Useful for AI + provenance:


manual


imported


ai-generated


transcript


web



5. Fields that should never be in the core
Keep these out of the universal base:


business-specific fields (estimate, amount, priority)


ownership (assignee)


scheduling (due-at)


relationships (parent, depends-on)


These belong in type-specific schemas, not the core.

6. Type-specific frontmatter (pattern)
Each type extends the core schema.
Example: task
type: task
priority: high
due-at: 2026-01-20T17:00:00Z
estimate: 2h
Your validator should:


enforce allowed fields per type


flag unknown fields


allow shared optional fields via $ref



7. Folder structure guidance (lightweight)
Folders are organizational hints, not identity.
Example:
_database/
  notes/
  tasks/
  docs/
  projects/

Rules:


Files may move freely between folders


Folder ≠ type (type lives in frontmatter)


Indexer must not infer meaning from path alone



8. Fixers you should ship on day one (naming + core FM)


Filename ↔ uid mismatch fixer


Missing uid → generate ULID + rename file


Missing created-at → fill from git or filesystem


Title missing → derive from first heading or filename


All with --dry-run first.

9. Summary (architectural stance)
Yes: ULID-only filenames.
Yes: small, universal frontmatter core.
Yes: type-specific schemas layered on top.
No: semantic filenames.
No: folder-as-meaning.
This gives you:


long-term stability


easy refactors


clean SQLite indexing


predictable AI retrieval


Obsidian ergonomics without lock-in


If you want, next we can:


lock down the status model per type


define the minimal global schema file


or design the ULID generation + rename strategy so adoption is painless.



Comments

Initial creation.

Framework v3 PRD
Version: 1.0.0
Status: Completed (2026-01-15)
Vision
A stable, scalable personal operating system where markdown is source of truth, SQLite enables fast queries, and ULID filenames eliminate refactoring friction.
Goals

Stability - ULID filenames make links rename-proof
Performance - SQLite index handles 10K+ files
Consistency - Unified schema with universal core
Tooling - CLI for index, validate, fix, doctor

Non-Goals

Obsidian plugin development
Multi-user support
Cloud sync features
Mobile-first workflows

Architecture
Markdown (source) → SQLite (derived) → Views (query)
     ↓                    ↓                 ↓
   Git-tracked        .gitignored       Obsidian/CLI

Invariant: SQLite is always rebuildable from markdown.
Core Changes
1. ULID-Only Filenames





















BeforeAftertask-127.md01JGFNLP8Z2XK4H7MZ9VYQ8C4A.mddoc-024.md01KF0N3VFC12P7FKSCSF75J1X5.mdsession-20260109-001.md01KEJET00A33X2BJ41W36Z9SNZ.md

Filename = ULID (no semantics)
Title lives in frontmatter
Links use ULID: [[01JGFNLP8Z]]

2. Universal Frontmatter Core
Required on every file:
type: note
title: Human-readable title
status: active
created-at: 2026-01-15T08:42:31Z
3. Unified Status Model

































StatusMeaningdraftWork in progressactiveCurrent, in useon-holdPausedcompletedDonearchivedRetained but inactivedeprecatedSuperseded
4. Schema Refactoring
_framework/schemas/
├── core.schema.json      # Universal fields
├── task.schema.json      # Extends core
├── doc.schema.json       # Extends core
├── session.schema.json   # Extends core
└── ...

5. SQLite Index
Tables:

files - All markdown files with frontmatter
tags - Tag relationships
links - Wikilink graph
errors - Validation issues

Generated by: MarkdownDB or custom indexer
6. CLI Tools
lexi index      # Rebuild SQLite from markdown
lexi validate   # Report errors, no changes
lexi fix        # Apply safe auto-fixes
lexi doctor     # Vault health summary
Deliverables
Phase 1: Foundation

 ULID filename migration script
 Universal core schema (11 split schemas created)
 Link updater (old → ULID refs)

Phase 2: Indexing

 SQLite indexer (custom Python implementation)
 Validation pipeline
 Error reporting

Phase 3: Tooling

 lexi CLI scaffold (4 commands)
 Safe fixers (timezone, missing fields, status)
 Health check integration

Phase 4: Migration

 Migrate existing 450 files
 Update Bases views
 Update CLAUDE.md workflows

Success Criteria

 All files use ULID filenames (450 files migrated)
 All files pass schema validation
 SQLite rebuilds in <1s for 450 files
 Zero broken wikilinks after migration
 CLI tools documented and working
 Unit tests added (113 tests passing)

Risks





















RiskMitigationObsidian alias handlingTest wikilink resolution with aliasesMigration data lossGit commit before each phasePerformance regressionBenchmark before/after

Knowledge

Phase 0: Preparation

git checkout -b v3-migration
git push -u origin v3-migration

find _database -name "*.md" > .migration/files-before.txt

├── links-before.txt

├── logs/
└── rollback/

Phase 1: Schema Foundation
1.1 Create Split Schema Files
_framework/schemas/

├── task.schema.json
├── backlog.schema.json
├── session.schema.json
├── project.schema.json

core.schema.json:
{
  "$schema": "json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "core-schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "uid": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[0-9A-HJKMNP-TV-Z]{26}$" },
    "type": { "type": "string" },

}
Type schemas use $ref:
{
  "$id": "task-schema",
  "allOf": [
    { "$ref": "core.schema.json" },
    {
      "properties": {
        "type": { "const": "task" },
        "priority": { "enum": ["0", "1", "2", "3"] },

1.2 Update Validator
# _framework/lib/schema_loader.py
def load_schema_for_type(entity_type: str) -> dict:
    schema_path = f"_framework/schemas/{entity_type}.schema.json"
    # Load with $ref resolution
1.3 Validation Checkpoint
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py --database core
# Must pass before proceeding
Phase 2: ULID Filename Migration
2.1 Build UID Mapping
# _framework/scripts/build-uid-mapping.py
import json
from pathlib import Path
from lib.validators import parse_markdown_frontmatter
 
mapping = {}
for md_file in Path('_database').rglob('*.md'):
    fm = parse_markdown_frontmatter(str(md_file))
    if 'uid' in fm:
        mapping[md_file.name] = {
            'uid': fm['uid'],
            'old_path': str(md_file),
            'new_path': str(md_file.parent / f"{fm['uid']}.md")
        }
 
with open('.migration/uid-mapping.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(mapping, f, indent=2)
2.2 Add Missing UIDs
Files without UIDs need them generated first:
# _framework/scripts/ensure-uids.py
# For each file missing uid:
#   1. Generate ULID
#   2. Add to frontmatter
#   3. Log change
2.3 Rename Files (Dry Run)
python3 _framework/scripts/rename-to-ulid.py --dry-run
# Output: Would rename 423 files
# Review changes before proceeding
2.4 Rename Files (Execute)
python3 _framework/scripts/rename-to-ulid.py --execute
git add -A
git commit -m "Rename all files to ULID filenames"
2.5 Update Wikilinks
# _framework/scripts/update-wikilinks.py
# For each file:
#   1. Find all [[old-filename]] references
#   2. Replace with [[ULID]]
#   3. Optionally add alias: [[ULID|display-name]]
python3 _framework/scripts/update-wikilinks.py --dry-run
python3 _framework/scripts/update-wikilinks.py --execute
git commit -m "Update all wikilinks to use ULID references"
2.6 Validation Checkpoint
# Verify no broken links
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py
grep -roh '\[\[.*\]\]' _database > .migration/links-after.txt
# Compare link counts
Phase 3: Frontmatter Normalization
3.1 Normalize Timestamps
# _framework/scripts/normalize-timestamps.py
# For each file:
#   1. Parse created-at
#   2. Ensure timezone present (default to -08:00)
#   3. Rewrite if changed
3.2 Normalize Status Values
Mapping:
STATUS_MAP = {
    # Task/Backlog
    'open': 'active',
    'not-started': 'draft',
    'in-progress': 'active',
    'someday': 'on-hold',
    'canceled': 'archived',
 
    # Keep as-is
    'draft': 'draft',
    'active': 'active',
    'completed': 'completed',
    'archived': 'archived',
}
3.3 Add Aliases (Optional)
# _framework/scripts/add-title-aliases.py
# For each file:
#   1. If no aliases field, add aliases: [title]
#   2. Enables [[ULID|Title]] resolution
3.4 Validation Checkpoint
python3 _framework/scripts/health-check.py
# All files must pass schema validation
Phase 4: SQLite Indexer
4.1 Choose Implementation
Option A: MarkdownDB (faster start)
npm install -g @markdowndb/cli
mddb _database --out .cache/markdown.db
Option B: Custom Python (more control)
# _framework/lib/indexer.py
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
 
def build_index(vault_path: str, db_path: str):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    conn.execute('''
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS files (
            uid TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            path TEXT,
            type TEXT,
            title TEXT,
            status TEXT,
            created_at TEXT,
            frontmatter JSON
        )
    ''')
    # ... index all files
4.2 Create Index Tables
-- files: core metadata
CREATE TABLE files (
    uid TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    path TEXT NOT NULL,
    type TEXT NOT NULL,
    title TEXT,
    status TEXT,
    created_at TEXT,
    frontmatter JSON
);
 
-- tags: many-to-many
CREATE TABLE tags (
    uid TEXT,
    tag TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (uid, tag),
    FOREIGN KEY (uid) REFERENCES files(uid)
);
 
-- links: wikilink graph
CREATE TABLE links (
    source_uid TEXT,
    target_uid TEXT,
    context TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (source_uid, target_uid),
    FOREIGN KEY (source_uid) REFERENCES files(uid)
);
 
-- errors: validation issues
CREATE TABLE errors (
    uid TEXT,
    error_type TEXT,
    message TEXT,
    fixable BOOLEAN,
    PRIMARY KEY (uid, error_type)
);
4.3 Add to .gitignore
# SQLite index (derived, rebuildable)
.cache/
*.db
markdown.db
4.4 Validation Checkpoint
python3 _framework/scripts/build-index.py
sqlite3 .cache/index.db "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM files"
# Should return 423
Phase 5: CLI Tooling
5.1 Create CLI Scaffold
_framework/cli/
├── __init__.py
├── main.py          # Entry point
├── index.py         # lexi index
├── validate.py      # lexi validate
├── fix.py           # lexi fix

5.2 Implement Commands
lexi index:
def cmd_index(args):
    """Rebuild SQLite index from markdown files."""
    build_index('_database', '.cache/index.db')
    print(f"Indexed {count} files")
lexi validate:
def cmd_validate(args):
    """Validate all files against schemas."""
    errors = validate_all()
    for e in errors:
        print(f"❌ {e.path}: {e.message}")
    return 1 if errors else 0
lexi fix:
def cmd_fix(args):
    """Apply safe auto-fixes."""
    if args.dry_run:
        print("Dry run - no changes")
    fixes = [
        fix_timezone_format,
        fix_status_normalization,

    # Apply fixes with confirmation
lexi doctor:
def cmd_doctor(args):
    """Print vault health summary."""
    print("=== Vault Health ===")
    print(f"Files: {file_count}")
    print(f"Valid: {valid_count}")
    print(f"Errors: {error_count}")
    print(f"Broken links: {broken_link_count}")
5.3 Add Entry Point
# Install as command
pip install -e _framework/
 
# Or use directly
python3 -m _framework.cli.main index
Phase 6: Update Workflows

type: note

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KF6.content:
Web Publishing Comparison and Recommendation
Comprehensive evaluation of options for publishing this Obsidian vault to the web.
Overview
This document evaluates web publishing platforms for the Personal Operating System vault, considering its unique characteristics: ULID-based filenames, Bases usage, framework code to exclude, and the goal of publishing most content publicly.
Decision Date: 2026-01-17
Recommendation: Quartz
Vault-Specific Requirements
Must Have





























RequirementRationaleULID filename supportAll files use ULID filenames (e.g., 01KF5ZF16NXG7V4EMHDY858CV8.md) with titles in frontmatterHuman-readable URLsVisitors need readable URLs, not ULID stringsSelective exclusionMust exclude _framework/, tmp/, .obsidian/, and private contentWikilink supportInternal links use [[ULID|Display Title]] formatFrontmatter title: supportPage titles come from frontmatter, not filenames
Nice to Have

































RequirementRationaleDataview renderingDynamic queries rendered as static contentGraph viewVisual representation of note connectionsFull-text searchVisitor search capabilityLocal previewTest site before publishingCustom stylingMatch personal aesthetic preferencesFree hostingMinimize ongoing costs
Known Limitations

















LimitationImpactNo Bases supportNo platform renders Bases views (as of Jan 2026)Dynamic contentAll platforms produce static sites; no live queries
Platform Comparison
Quick Reference


















































































FeatureObsidian PublishQuartzDigital GardenFlowershowCost$100/yearFreeFreeFree / $50/yrSetup EffortMinimalModerateModerateEasyULID/Permalink✓ permalink:✓ permalink:✓ dg-permalink:UnknownBases Support✗✗✗✗DataviewPlugin workaroundQuartz Syncer✓ Native✗Graph View✓✓✓✗Full-text Search✓✓✓PremiumLocal Preview✗✓Limited✗Custom StylingLimitedFullModerateFullBulk PublishingGoodExcellentPoorGood
Detailed Analysis
Obsidian Publish
Overview: Official first-party publishing service from Obsidian.
Pros:

Zero configuration required
Native Obsidian integration
Automatic updates when vault changes
Custom domain support
Password protection available
Graph view and hover previews

Cons:

$100/year ongoing cost
No Bases support (confirmed “not yet” by moderators)
Limited customization options
No local preview capability
Vendor lock-in

ULID Handling:
permalink: my-readable-url
The permalink: frontmatter field overrides the filename-based URL.
Best For: Users who want zero-friction setup and don’t mind the cost.
Documentation: help.obsidian.md/publish

Quartz
Overview: Free, open-source static site generator designed for Obsidian vaults.
Pros:

Completely free
Highly customizable (full template control)
Excellent for bulk publishing
Local development server for preview
Strong community and active development
ignorePatterns for excluding private content
Quartz Syncer plugin compiles Dataview to static
Graph view, backlinks, full-text search included

Cons:

Requires Node.js and Git knowledge
More complex initial setup
No Bases support
Filters only work on markdown (non-md files need manual exclusion)

ULID Handling:
title: My Readable Title
permalink: my-readable-url
If no permalink:, Quartz uses title: property. Falls back to filename if neither exists.
Exclusion Configuration:
// quartz.config.ts
ignorePatterns: [
  "_framework/**",
  ".obsidian/**",
  "tmp/**",
  "**/*.py",
  "**/*.json",
]
Best For: Technical users publishing most of their vault who want full control.
Documentation: quartz.jzhao.xyz/

Digital Garden
Overview: Free Obsidian plugin for selective note publishing via GitHub and Vercel.
Pros:

Free hosting
Native Dataview support (best of all options)
Fine-grained publish control via frontmatter
dg-permalink: for custom URLs
Supports graph view, backlinks, search

Cons:

Requires marking each note with dg-publish: true
Poor fit for “publish most” use case (must mark hundreds of files)
No local preview
No Bases support
Moderate setup complexity

ULID Handling:
dg-publish: true
dg-permalink: "my-readable-url"
Best For: Selective publishing (cherry-pick specific notes).
Documentation: dg-docs.ole.dev/

Flowershow
Overview: Hosted platform evolved from a Next.js template, now offering managed publishing.
Pros:

Easy setup with managed hosting
Good blogging features (author profiles, comments)
Cheaper than Obsidian Publish ($50/year premium)
Custom domain support

Cons:

No Dataview support
No graph view
No Bases support
Full-text search only on premium
Less documented permalink handling
Less mature than other options

Best For: Blog-style publishing with minimal technical overhead.
Documentation: flowershow.app/
Recommendation: Quartz
Why Quartz
For publishing most of the vault with private exclusions, Quartz is the best fit:













































FactorAssessmentBulk publishing modelPublish all, exclude specific paths - matches use caseULID supportpermalink: + title: frontmatter work wellCostFree (GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Vercel hosting)Technical fitVault owner comfortable with Python/CLI; Node.js won’t be an issueFramework exclusionignorePatterns cleanly excludes _framework/**DataviewQuartz Syncer can compile queries to static contentLocal previewTest full site before publishingCustomizationFull control over templates and stylingCommunityActive development, good documentation
Why Not Others





















PlatformReason Not RecommendedObsidian Publish$100/year for features available free elsewhereDigital GardenRequires marking every published file; poor for bulkFlowershowNo Dataview, no graph view, less mature
Implementation Plan
Phase 1: Setup


Install prerequisites
node --version  # Requires v22+
npm --version   # Requires v10.9.2+


Clone Quartz
git clone github.com/jackyzha0/quartz.git
cd quartz
npm i
npx quartz create


Configure exclusions in quartz.config.ts:
ignorePatterns: [
  "_framework/**",
  ".obsidian/**",
  "tmp/**",
  ".cache/**",
  "tests/**",
  "**/*.py",
  "**/*.json",
  "**/README.md",  // Framework READMEs
]


Configure content source to point to vault


Phase 2: URL Strategy
Option A: Auto-generate from title (recommended)

Quartz uses title: frontmatter for URLs by default
“My Note Title” becomes /my-note-title
No additional frontmatter needed

Option B: Explicit permalinks

Add permalink: only where custom URL needed
Useful for frequently-shared links that must remain stable

Recommendation: Start with Option A, add explicit permalinks only for high-traffic pages.
Phase 3: Private Content
For individual private notes within public folders:
draft: true  # Excludes from Quartz build
Phase 4: Dataview Migration
Since Bases aren’t supported anywhere, consider:

Identify Bases views that should appear on public site
Convert to Dataview queries
Install Quartz Syncer plugin to compile to static

Phase 5: Hosting
Recommended: GitHub Pages (free, simple)
Alternatives:

Netlify (free tier, automatic deploys)
Vercel (free tier, fast)
Cloudflare Pages (free, global CDN)

Phase 6: Custom Domain (Optional)
Configure DNS and update Quartz config for custom domain.
Future Considerations
Bases Support
Monitor these sources for Bases publishing support:

Obsidian Publish roadmap: help.obsidian.md/bases/roadmap
Obsidian Forum: forum.obsidian.md/t/do-bases-work-with-obsidian-publish/106703
Quartz GitHub issues

If Obsidian Publish adds Bases support before Quartz, re-evaluate recommendation.
Alternative: Dataview Publisher
If Dataview is sufficient (instead of Bases), the Dataview Publisher plugin renders queries to markdown for any platform.
Static Bases Rendering
A potential community solution could compile Bases views to static tables at build time, similar to how Quartz Syncer handles Dataview.
File Handling Reference
What Gets Published





























File TypeBehaviorMarkdown (.md)Published with syntax highlightingImagesCopied to output, embedded in pagesPDFCopied if not in ignorePatternsCanvasConverted to visual pagePython/JSON/CodeIgnored (via ignorePatterns)
Code in Notes
Code blocks within markdown render with syntax highlighting:
```python
def hello():
    print("Hello, world!")
```
This works on all platforms.
Properties for Publishing
Recommended Schema Addition
Add these optional properties for publishing workflow:
# Publishing properties (optional)
publish: boolean      # Explicit publish flag (for filtered publishing)
draft: boolean        # Exclude from build (Quartz)
permalink: string     # URL path override
Auto-Generated URL Behavior





















Property PresentURL Generatedpermalink: custom-url/custom-urltitle: My Page/my-pageNeither/01KF61MH10Q8V8SDB0H4728VWA (filename)

Sources

Quartz: quartz.jzhao.xyz/
Digital Garden: dg-docs.ole.dev/

_database/database-docs/docs-table/01KF7.content:
PRD: Web Publishing with Quartz
Overview
Publish selected vault content as a public digital garden using Quartz static site generator and GitHub Pages.
Current State

Quartz setup: Complete, local builds working
Live URL: tomboo.github.io/quartz-site/
Repo: github.com/tomboo/quartz-site
Privacy: draft: true excludes content from build
Deploy: npm run deploy from quartz-site directory

Problem Statement
Bases views (our primary data display mechanism) don’t render in Quartz. Published pages with .base files or Bases syntax show raw code instead of interactive tables. This breaks the experience for any “app” content we want to publish (YouTube queue, reading lists, project dashboards).
Requirements
P0 - Must Have

























IDRequirementNotesR1Static table generationPre-render Bases/Dataview queries to markdown tables at build timeR2Content curationClear strategy for public vs private contentR3Privacy by defaultAll content private unless explicitly marked for publish
P1 - Should Have

























IDRequirementNotesR4Friendly URLsPermalink property for human-readable pathsR5Custom domainnotes.tomboo.com or similar subdomainR6Theme customizationMatch personal brand/preferences
P2 - Nice to Have




















IDRequirementNotesR7Automated deployScript or hook to deploy after session commitsR8Build validationCheck for broken links before deploy
Proposed Solution: Static Table Generation
Option A: Quartz Syncer Plugin
quartz-syncer converts Dataview queries to static markdown. Could be adapted for Bases.
Pros: Community solution, Quartz-native
Cons: Dataview-focused, may not support Bases syntax
Option B: Build-time Script
Custom Python script that:

Reads .base files and parses filter syntax
Queries SQLite index for matching files
Generates static markdown tables
Outputs to _generated/ folder for Quartz to include

Pros: Full control, uses existing SQLite index, Bases-native
Cons: Custom maintenance, needs filter parser
Option C: Manual Curation
Don’t publish dynamic views. Instead:

Publish individual notes only
Create curated “index” pages with manual links
Skip apps/dashboards entirely

Pros: Simple, no tooling needed
Cons: Defeats purpose of structured data, high maintenance
Recommendation
Option B - Build-time script leveraging our existing infrastructure:

SQLite index already has all file metadata
Bases filter syntax is documented
Can generate clean markdown tables
Integrates with existing npm run deploy workflow

Content Curation Strategy
Publish (opt-in)
Add publish: true to frontmatter:

Selected notes (technical references, guides)
Public projects
Reading lists, recommendations

Private (default)
Everything without publish: true:

Sessions, tasks, backlog
Daily notes
Personal projects
Drafts

Implementation
Modify Quartz config to filter on publish: true instead of draft: true:
// quartz.config.ts
Plugin.FrontMatter(),
Plugin.FilterPublished(), // Custom: only include publish: true
Technical Architecture
vault-personal-tom/
├── _database/
│   ├── content-storage/     # Media, transcripts
│   └── database-core/       # Notes, projects, etc.

quartz-site/
├── content/                 # Symlink to vault OR
│   └── _generated/          # Static tables from build script
├── quartz.config.ts         # Quartz configuration
└── scripts/
    └── generate-tables.py   # Bases → markdown converter

Build Workflow
# 1. Generate static tables from Bases views
python3 scripts/generate-tables.py
 
# 2. Build and deploy Quartz
npm run deploy
Success Criteria

 Public site shows only publish: true content
 At least one “app view” (e.g., reading list) renders as static table
 No sensitive/personal content exposed
 Deploy takes < 2 minutes

Open Questions

Should we symlink vault or copy files to quartz content?
Which Bases views are worth publishing?
How often to rebuild/deploy?

References

Web Publishing Project
Quartz Tutorial (Nicole)
Quartz Tutorial (isak)

Docs Component
Version: 1.0.0

Framework: v2
Purpose
The Docs component manages technical documentation, guides, how-tos, and reference materials. It provides a structured way to create, organize, and maintain documentation within the vault.
Database

Schema
Required Properties

Recommended Properties













































PropertyTypeDescriptiondatedateCreation or reference date (YYYY-MM-DD)userstringDocument owner (kebab-case)descriptionstringBrief 1-line summary for search/listingssynopsisstring2-3 sentence summary (50-500 chars)categorystringDocument category (kebab-case)tagsarrayDocument tagscreated-atdatetimeCreation timestamp (ISO 8601)
Synopsis Guidelines
The synopsis property provides a 2-3 sentence summary that:

Explains the document’s purpose and main content
Helps readers quickly understand what they’ll learn
Is longer than description but still concise (50-500 characters)

Example:
description: Framework v2 architecture overview.
synopsis: This document describes the v2 architecture with self-contained databases, JSON Schema validation, and portable components. It covers the directory structure, migration path from v1, and design principles for multi-vault support.
Optional Properties























































PropertyTypeDescriptiondoc-typeenumprd, plan, guide, reference, spec, notes, tutorial, changelogprojectwikilinkLink to parent projectareawikilinkLink to life/work arearelatedarrayLinks to related documentsaudienceenuminternal, team, publicversionstringDocument version (semver: 1.0 or 1.0.0)sourceenumoriginal, notion, migration, importsource-urluriOriginal URL if migratedreviewed-atdatetimeLast review/verification timestamp
Wikilink Convention
Use the alias format for human-readable frontmatter:
# Recommended: with alias
project: "[[../projects-table/project-framework-v2|Framework v2]]"
area: "[[../areas-table/area-technical|Technical]]"
related:
  - "[[doc-001|Framework v2 Architecture]]"
  - "[[doc-003|Framework v2 PRD]]"
 
# Avoid: without alias (hard to read)
project: "[[../projects-table/project-framework-v2]]"
Note: Obsidian updates file paths on rename but not aliases. Accept minor sync risk for readability.
Status Workflow
draft → active → archived
              ↘ deprecated


draft: Work in progress, not finalized
active: Current, maintained documentation
archived: Historical, no longer maintained
deprecated: Superseded, kept for reference

Views

Tabs in docs-base.base:

grep -l "slug: prd-framework-v2" _database/database-docs/docs-table/
